arXiv:1804.08776v3 [math-ph] 03 Dec 2019

Enhanced group classification
of nonlinear diffusion–reaction equations
with gradient-dependent diffusivity

Stanislav Opanasenko†§, Vyacheslav Boyko§ and Roman O. Popovych‡§

†Department of Mathematics and Statistics, Memorial University of Newfoundland,
 St. John’s (NL) A1C 5S7, Canada

‡Fakultät für Mathematik, Universität Wien, Oskar-Morgenstern-Platz 1, 1090 Wien, Austria  & Mathematical Institute, Silesian University in Opava, Na Rybníčku 1, 746 01 Opava,
 Czech Republic

§Institute of Mathematics of NAS of Ukraine, 3 Tereshchenkivs’ka Str., 01004 Kyiv, Ukraine

E-mail: sopanasenko@mun.ca, boyko@imath.kiev.ua, rop@imath.kiev.ua

We carry out the enhanced group classification of a class of (1+1)-dimensional nonlinear diffusion–reaction equations with gradient-dependent diffusivity using the two-step version of the method of furcate splitting. For simultaneously finding the equivalence groups of an unnormalized class of differential equations and a collection of its subclasses, we suggest an optimized version of the direct method. The optimization includes the preliminary study of admissible transformations within the entire class and the successive splitting of the corresponding determining equations with respect to arbitrary elements and their derivatives depending on auxiliary constraints associated with each of required subclasses. In the course of applying the suggested technique to subclasses of the class under consideration, we construct, for the first time, a nontrivial example of finite-dimensional effective generalized equivalence group. Using the method of Lie reduction and the generalized separation of variables, exact solutions of some equations under consideration are found.

1 Introduction

The recent researches in biology showed that diffusion–reaction equations draw an attention as a prototype model for pattern formation. The various patterns, such as fronts, spirals, targets etc., can be found in various types of diffusion–reaction systems depending on large discrepancies [24, 25]. The latest application of diffusion–reaction processes are connected to process of morphogenesis as well as can be relevant to animal coats and skin pigmentation [16]. Among other applications are ecological invasions, spread of epidemics, tumour growth and wound healing [45].

The initial purpose of the present paper was the group classification of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} of (1+1)-dimensional diffusion–reaction equations with a gradient-dependent diffusivity,

ut=f⁡(ux)​ux​x+g⁡(u),u_{t}=f(u_{x})u_{xx}+g(u), (1)

where f=f⁡(ux)f=f(u_{x}) and g=g⁡(u)g=g(u) are smooth functions of their arguments with f≠0f\neq 0. This problem had been considered in [8] with several weaknesses (see the conclusion of the present paper), which made necessary to accurately study it once more. Using the classical method of Lie reduction and other techniques, we also planned to construct exact solutions of equations from the regular subclass of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} that are the most interesting from the Lie-symmetry point of view.

According to the formalized definition of a class of differential equations [35, 39], the complete system of auxiliary equations and inequalities for the arbitrary elements ff and gg of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is given by

ft=fx=fu=fut=fut​t=fut​x=fux​x=0,f≠0,gt=gx=gut=gux=gut​t=gut​x=gux​x=0.\displaystyle\begin{split}&f_{t}=f_{x}=f_{u}=f_{u_{t}}=f_{u_{tt}}=f_{u_{tx}}=f_{u_{xx}}=0,\quad f\neq 0,\\ &g_{t}=g_{x}=g_{u_{t}}=g_{u_{x}}=g_{u_{tt}}=g_{u_{tx}}=g_{u_{xx}}=0.\end{split} (2)

The structure of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is not nice from the point of view of equivalence transformations and Lie symmetries. This is why it is convenient to represent this class as a union of four subclasses,

ℛ=ℋ∪ℒ∪ℱ∪𝒞.\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{F}\cup\mathcal{C}.

The subclass ℋ\mathcal{H} of semilinear equations (called “nonlinear heat equations with source”) is singled out by the constraint fux=0f_{u_{x}}=0. This class includes all linear equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, which additionally satisfy the constraint gu​u=0g_{uu}=0 and are reduced by simple point transformations to the linear heat equation ut=ux​xu_{t}=u_{xx}. The complete group classification of the subclass ℋ\mathcal{H} was carried out in [10] in the course of the group classification of the wider class of diffusion–reaction equations of the general form ut=f⁡(u)​ux​x+g⁡(u)u_{t}=f(u)u_{xx}+g(u) with f≠0f\neq 0. See also [3, pp. 133–136] for an enhanced representation of these results.

The subclass ℒ\mathcal{L} consists of equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, where the values of the arbitrary element ff satisfy the constraint (ux​f2)ux=0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}=0. The subclass ℒ\mathcal{L} is special because each equation from it can be linearized to a Kolmogorov equation. More specifically, the hodograph transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=u\tilde{x}=u, u~=x\tilde{u}=x with (t~,x~)(\tilde{t},\tilde{x}) and u~\tilde{u} being the new independent and dependent variables, respectively, maps an equation of the form (1), where f=c​ux−2f=cu_{x}^{-2} with c=const≠0c={\rm const}\neq 0, to the Kolmogorov equation

u~t~=c​u~x~​x~−g⁡(x~)​u~x~.\displaystyle\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=c\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}-g(\tilde{x})\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}. (3)

In particular, this means that the subclass ℒ\mathcal{L} has completely different point-transformation and Lie-symmetry properties in comparison with the other subclasses, and its group classification reduces to the group classification of the class of Kolmogorov equations, which was presented, e.g., in [40, Corollary 7] up to general point equivalence.

The subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} is singled out by the constraint gu=0g_{u}=0. The singularity of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} is exhibited by properties of its equivalence transformations, see Section 2. In particular, the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} admits an extension of equivalence group in comparison with the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R}, and it is mapped by a family of its equivalence transformations to its subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} associated with the additional constraint g=0g=0. Thus, the group classification of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} reduces to the group classification of the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. The latter subclass consists of “nonlinear filtration equations”, which are of the form (1) with f≠0f\neq 0 and g=0g=0. The group classification of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} was carried out in [1, 2]. Lists of inequivalent Lie-symmetry extensions in this class up to its complete equivalence group and up to a proper subgroup of this group can also be singled out from the corresponding lists for potential diffusion–convection equations, presented in [38], by selecting cases with the zero convection coefficient.

Each of the additional auxiliary constraints associated with subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℱ\mathcal{F} is related to a special case of solving the group classification problem for the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. This is why we call the complement 𝒞\mathcal{C} of ℋ∪ℒ∪ℱ\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{F} in ℛ\mathcal{R} the regular subclass of ℛ\mathcal{R}. It is associated, as a subclass of ℛ\mathcal{R}, with the system of the inequalities fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0, (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 and gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0.

Note that the union of the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℱ\mathcal{F} is not disjoint since there are two nonempty intersections among the pairwise intersections of these subclasses, ℋ∩ℱ\mathcal{H}\cap\mathcal{F} and ℒ∩ℱ\mathcal{L}\cap\mathcal{F}. Unfortunately, there is no partition of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} into subclasses that is convenient for group classification. For example, the equivalence group of the subclass ℱ∖(ℋ∪ℒ)\mathcal{F}\setminus(\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{L}) is merely a proper subgroup of the equivalence group of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}, which essentially complicates the group classification of ℱ∖(ℋ∪ℒ)\mathcal{F}\setminus(\mathcal{H}\cup\mathcal{L}) in comparison with ℱ\mathcal{F}.

Although the group classifications for the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and ℱ\mathcal{F} are in fact known, the complete exclusion of these subclasses from the consideration, as this was done in [8], is not natural. Thus, there are point transformations mapping equations from the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} to equations from the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and related Lie-symmetry extensions in ℱ\mathcal{F} are simpler than their counterparts in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The same claim is true for the subclass pair (ℒ,ℋ)(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{H}). Therefore, to solve the group classification problem for the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, we carry out the group classification of the regular subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} using the technique of furcate splitting [17, 26, 48], combine the result with the known group classification of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} and supplement it with the additional inequivalent cases of Lie-symmetry extension from the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℒ\mathcal{L}.

As mentioned above, the initial purpose of the present paper was to correctly solve the group classification problem for the class ℛ\mathcal{R} but it was changed after the careful analysis of admissible and equivalence transformations within this class. The generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} turns out to be nontrivial, and using it as a conditional generalized equivalence group of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} simplifies the computation in the course of the group classification of this class and makes it more consistent with the subclass hierarchy considered for the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. We also constructed an effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}, which is perhaps the most interesting and unexpected result of the paper since it gives the first example of nontrivial finite-dimensional effective generalized equivalence group in the literature. Moreover, the group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is a proper but not normal subgroup of the group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, and hence it is not a unique effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} the class ℱ\mathcal{F}. One more interesting feature of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is that its usual equivalence group is contained in no effective generalized equivalence group of this class.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we simultaneously compute the equivalence groups of the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R} and of the above subclasses of this class using an original optimized version of the direct method. The classification of Lie symmetries of equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is presented in Section 3. Section 4 contains the first comprehensive description of the method of furcate splitting. The two-step version of this method is used in Section 5 to solve, as a part of the group classification problem for the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R}, the group classification problem for its regular subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}. In Section 6, we select the three most interesting cases in the classification list obtained for the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} and construct exact solutions of the related equations using Lie reduction or the generalized separation of variables. Results of the paper are discussed in Section 7.

2 Equivalence transformations

For simultaneously finding the equivalence groups of an unnormalized class of differential equations and a collection of its subclasses, we suggest an optimized version of the direct method, which involves the preliminary study of admissible transformations within the entire class and the successive splitting of the determining equations for these transformations with respect to the corresponding arbitrary elements and their derivatives, depending on auxiliary constraints associated with each of required subclasses.

By definition, equivalence transformations for the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and its subclasses are point transformations in the joint space of the independent variables (t,x)(t,x), the dependent variable uu, its first- and second-order derivatives and the arbitrary elements ff and gg. Due to specific form of the arbitrary elements ff and gg, these transformations can be defined on spaces with a smaller number of coordinates; cf. [28]. Since the arbitrary element ff depends on uxu_{x}, this derivative should be among the coordinates of such a space although the corresponding transformation components can still be computed from the xx- and uu-components using the chain rule. Due to the evolution form of equations, the derivative utu_{t} is not involved in the transformation components for uxu_{x} and thus can be excluded from the coordinates of such a space. As a result, the minimal list of coordinates for a space underlying equivalence transformations for the classes ℛ\mathcal{R}, ℒ\mathcal{L}, ℱ\mathcal{F} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} is (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g). (The uxu_{x}-component of equivalence transformations was missed in [8, Theorem 2].) Since the subclass ℋ\mathcal{H} is associated with the constraint fux=0f_{u_{x}}=0, the coordinate uxu_{x} can be neglected when defining equivalence transformations of this subclass but for unification we will not use this possibility. At the same time, in view of the constraint g=0g=0 it is convenient to exclude the gg-component when defining equivalence transformations of the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}.

In order to compute the equivalence groups of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and its subclasses in a uniform way, we begin this computation with the preliminary study of admissible transformations in this class. Since the class ℛ\mathcal{R} consists of (1+1)-dimensional second-order evolution equations whose right hand sides are affine in the derivative ux​xu_{xx}, any contact admissible transformation in this class is a prolongation of a point admissible transformation [41]. Moreover, the tt-component of any admissible transformation within ℛ\mathcal{R} depends only on tt; see the related assertions in [19] and [18] for contact and point transformations between (1+1)-dimensional evolution equations, respectively. Therefore, we consider a point transformation of independent and dependent variables of the form

t~=T⁡(t),x~=X⁡(t,x,u),u~=U⁡(t,x,u),\displaystyle\tilde{t}=T(t),\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=X(t,x,u),\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=U(t,x,u), (4)

where Tt​(Xx​Uu−Xu​Ux)≠0T_{t}(X_{x}U_{u}-X_{u}U_{x})\neq 0, that connects the source and the target equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R},

ut=f⁡(ux)​ux​x+g⁡(u)andu~t~=f~​(u~x~)​u~x~​x~+g~​(u~).\displaystyle u_{t}=f(u_{x})u_{xx}+g(u)\hskip 10.00002pt\text{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}=\tilde{f}(\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}})\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}}+\tilde{g}(\tilde{u}). (5)

Proceeding with the direct method of finding the equivalence groupoid of a class of equations, we write the differentiation operators ∂t~\partial_{\tilde{t}} and ∂x~\partial_{\tilde{x}} with respect to new independent variables in terms of old ones as

∂t~=1Tt(Dt−Dt​XDx​XDx),∂x~=1Dx​XDx,\partial_{\tilde{t}}=\frac{1}{T_{t}}\left(\mathrm{D}_{t}-\frac{\mathrm{D}_{t}X}{\mathrm{D}_{x}X}\mathrm{D}_{x}\right),\hskip 10.00002pt\partial_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{D}_{x}X}\mathrm{D}_{x},

We substitute the expressions for u~\tilde{u}, u~t~\tilde{u}_{\tilde{t}}, u~x~\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}} and u~x~​x~\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}\tilde{x}} in terms of old variables into the target equation,

replace utu_{t} by f​ux​x+gfu_{xx}+g and successively split the equation obtained with respect to ux​xu_{xx}. This results in “expressions” for the target arbitrary elements f~\tilde{f} and g~\tilde{g},

f~​(V)=(Dx​X)2Tt​f​(ux),\displaystyle\tilde{f}(V)=\frac{(\mathrm{D}_{x}X)^{2}}{T_{t}}f(u_{x}), (6)

where Δ:=Xx​Uu−Xu​Ux≠0\Delta:=X_{x}U_{u}-X_{u}U_{x}\neq 0. Since both the source and target arbitrary-element tuples satisfy the auxiliary system (2), the equations (6) and (7) imply further determining equations for admissible transformations in the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. There are two ways for deriving these determining equations.

The first way is to express the operators ∂t~\partial_{\tilde{t}}, ∂x~\partial_{\tilde{x}}, ∂u~\partial_{\tilde{u}} and ∂u~x~\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} in terms of the operators ∂t\partial_{t}, ∂x\partial_{x}, ∂u\partial_{u} and ∂ux\partial_{u_{x}}, which act on functions of (t,x,u,ux)(t,x,u,u_{x}), using the equalities implied by the chain rule for these operators:

∂t=Tt∂t~+Xt∂x~+Ut∂u~+Vt∂u~x~,∂x=Xx∂x~+Ux∂u~+Vx∂u~x~,∂u=Xu∂x~+Uu∂u~+Vu∂u~x~,∂ux=Vux∂u~x~.\displaystyle\partial_{t}=T_{t}\partial_{\tilde{t}}+X_{t}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+U_{t}\partial_{\tilde{u}}+V_{t}\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}},\hskip 10.00002pt\begin{array}[]{l}\partial_{x}=X_{x}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+U_{x}\partial_{\tilde{u}}+V_{x}\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}},\\[4.30554pt] \partial_{u}=X_{u}\partial_{\tilde{x}}+U_{u}\partial_{\tilde{u}}+V_{u}\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}},\end{array}\hskip 10.00002pt\partial_{u_{x}}=V_{u_{x}}\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}}.

Then one acts by the operators ∂t~\partial_{\tilde{t}}, ∂x~\partial_{\tilde{x}} and ∂u~\partial_{\tilde{u}} on the equation (6) and the operators ∂t~\partial_{\tilde{t}}, ∂x~\partial_{\tilde{x}} and ∂u~x~\partial_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} on the equation (7). The determining equations derived in this way are appropriate in order to solve the problem of describing the equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℛ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} of the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. This problem is reduced to the classification of admissible transformations, which is similar to but more complicated than the classification of Lie symmetries in Sections 3 and 5 below. It is not a subject of the present paper although we will need a partial classification of admissible transformations for proving Theorem 13.

We use the other way, which gives more compact determining equations for equivalence transformations. We solve the equations (6) and (7) with respect to ff and gg, respectively,

f⁡(ux)=Tt(Dx​X)2​f~​(V),\displaystyle f(u_{x})=\frac{T_{t}}{(\mathrm{D}_{x}X)^{2}}\tilde{f}(V), (8)

(We divided the last equation by TtT_{t}.) Since the tt-, xx- and uu-components of usual equivalence transformations do not depend on the arbitrary elements ff and gg, in the course of computing the usual equivalence groups of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and its subclasses we can split the classifying equations (10)–(12) with respect to all parametric derivatives of the target arbitrary elements including f~\tilde{f} and g~\tilde{g} themselves. At the same time, the complete system of classifying equations for admissible transformations within a subclass of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} may be more restrictive than the equations (10)–(12); see the proofs of propositions below.

Remark 1.

Each equivalence transformation of any subclass of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is completely defined by its the tt-, xx- and uu-components. Indeed, if these components are known, then the uxu_{x}-component is computed by the chain rule, and the expressions for ff- and gg-components follow from the equations (6) and (7). This is why we do not discuss the derivation of the latter expressions below.

Proposition 2.

The usual equivalence group Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} coincides with the usual equivalence groups of its subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} and consists of the point transformations in the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g), whose components are of the form

t~=T1t+T0,x~=X1x+X0,u~=U2u+U0,u~x~=U2X1ux,f~=X1 2T1f,g~=U2T1g,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=T_{1}t+T_{0},\quad\tilde{x}=X_{1}x+X_{0},\quad\tilde{u}=U_{2}u+U_{0},\quad\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{U_{2}}{X_{1}}u_{x},\\ &\tilde{f}=\frac{X_{1}^{\,2}}{T_{1}}f,\quad\tilde{g}=\frac{U_{2}}{T_{1}}g,\end{split} (13)

where TT’s, XX’s and UU’s are arbitrary constants with T1​X1​U2≠0T_{1}X_{1}U_{2}\not=0.

Proof.

For each of the classes ℛ\mathcal{R}, ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the arbitrary element g~\tilde{g} and its derivative g~u~\tilde{g}_{\tilde{u}} are not constrained. Collecting the coefficients of g~u~\tilde{g}_{\tilde{u}} and g~\tilde{g} in the equations (11) and (12), respectively, gives the determining equations Ut=Ux=0U_{t}=U_{x}=0 and Xu=0X_{u}=0. Therefore, Xx​Uu≠0X_{x}U_{u}\neq 0 and V=ux​Uu/XxV=u_{x}U_{u}/X_{x}. Then we split the equation (11) with y=ty=t with respect to g~\tilde{g} and derive Tt​t=0T_{tt}=0. The arbitrary element f~\tilde{f} can also be assumed as a parametric value for splitting, and its derivative f~u~x~\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} is either unconstrained or equal to zero or −2f~/u~x~-2\tilde{f}/\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}. This is why we can select terms without arbitrary elements and their derivatives in the equation (12), which leads to Xt=0X_{t}=0.

Now we only need to obtain the equations Xx​x=0X_{xx}=0 and Uu​u=0U_{uu}=0, which is done by considering separately cases with different constraints for f~\tilde{f}. Then the tt-, xx- and uu-components of usual equivalence transformations have precisely the form (13), and further we follow Remark 1. All the constructed transformations preserve each of the systems of auxiliary constraints for the arbitrary elements that are associated with the classes ℛ\mathcal{R}, ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

In particular, the values of f~\tilde{f} and f~u~x~\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} are not constrained by equations in the classes ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This allows us to split with respect to these values and get the equations Vz=0V_{z}=0, which are expanded, for z=xz=x and z=uz=u to the requested equations Xx​x=0X_{xx}=0 and Uu​u=0U_{uu}=0, respectively.

In view of the constraint f~u~x~=0\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}}=0 for the class ℋ\mathcal{H}, the equation (10) with z=xz=x and the equation (12) respectively reduce to Xx​x=0X_{xx}=0 and Vu+Vx​ux+ux​Vu​ux=0V_{u}+V_{xu_{x}}+u_{x}V_{uu_{x}}=0. The expansion of the last equation implies Uu​u=0U_{uu}=0.

Since f~u~x~=−2f~/u~x~≠0\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}}=-2\tilde{f}/\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}\neq 0 within the class ℒ\mathcal{L}, the equation (10) with z=uz=u is then equivalent to Vu=0V_{u}=0, i.e., Uu​u=0U_{uu}=0, and the equation (12) reduces to Xx​x=0X_{xx}=0. ∎

Solving the additional auxiliary equation (ux​f2)ux=0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}=0 for the arbitrary element ff in the subclass ℒ\mathcal{L}, we obtain the representation f=c​ux−2f=cu_{x}^{-2} with an arbitrary nonzero constant cc. If we reparameterize the subclass ℒ\mathcal{L} by taking this constant as a new arbitrary element instead of ff, then the corresponding transformation component is c~=U2 2​T1−1​c\tilde{c}=U_{2}^{\,2}T_{1}^{-1}c.

Proposition 3.

The usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is constituted by the point transformations in the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g), whose components are of the form

t~=T1t+T0,x~=X1x+X0,u~=U1x+U2u+U3t+U0,u~x~=U1+U2​uxX1,f~=(X1)2T1f,g~=U2T1g+U3T1,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=T_{1}t+T_{0},\quad\tilde{x}=X_{1}x+X_{0},\quad\tilde{u}=U_{1}x+U_{2}u+U_{3}t+U_{0},\quad\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{U_{1}+U_{2}u_{x}}{X_{1}},\\ &\tilde{f}=\frac{(X_{1})^{2}}{T_{1}}f,\quad\tilde{g}=\frac{U_{2}}{T_{1}}g+\frac{U_{3}}{T_{1}},\end{split} (14)

where TT’s, XX’s and UU’s are arbitrary constants with T1​X1​U2≠0T_{1}X_{1}U_{2}\neq 0.

Proof.

For the class ℱ\mathcal{F} we should extend the system of the classifying equations (10)–(12) with one more equation by replacing the subscript yy by zz in the equation (11), which takes into account the additional auxiliary constraint gu=0g_{u}=0 of this class. Then we substitute g~u~=0\tilde{g}_{\tilde{u}}=0 into the extended system and split it with respect to the varying values g~\tilde{g}, f~\tilde{f} and f~u~x~\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}}. Thus, vanishing the coefficient of g~\tilde{g} and the term without the varying values in the equation (12) results in the equations Xu=0X_{u}=0 (and hence Xx​Uu≠0X_{x}U_{u}\neq 0) and Xt=0X_{t}=0. From the equation (10) we derive Vz=0V_{z}=0 and Tt​t=0T_{tt}=0. We successively expand the equations Vz=0V_{z}=0 for z=tz=t, z=uz=u and z=xz=x and split them with respect to uxu_{x}, obtaining

Ut​x=Ut​u=0,Ux​u=Uu​u=0andXx​x=Ux​x=0,U_{tx}=U_{tu}=0,\hskip 10.00002ptU_{xu}=U_{uu}=0\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002ptX_{xx}=U_{xx}=0,

respectively. Then terms in the equation (11) without the varying values merely give Ut​t=0U_{tt}=0. The obtained equations for the transformations components constitute the complete system of determining equations for usual equivalence transformations of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} since the extended version of the system (10)–(12) is identically satisfied in view of the collection of these equations. Therefore, the components of all transformations from the group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} are of the form (14) and each transformation whose components are of the form (14) belongs to this group. ∎

The group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is a nontrivial conditional usual equivalence group of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} under the condition gu=0g_{u}=0 since the usual equivalence group Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is a proper subgroup of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which is singled out by the constraints U1=U3=0U_{1}=U_{3}=0 for group parameters. Elements of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} with (U1,U3)≠(0,0)(U_{1},U_{3})\neq(0,0) are purely conditional equivalence transformations for the class ℛ\mathcal{R} under the condition gu=0g_{u}=0.

The family of transformations from Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} with (t,x,u)(t,x,u)-components t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=x\tilde{x}=x, u~=u−g​t\tilde{u}=u-gt, which is parameterized by the arbitrary element gg, maps the class ℱ\mathcal{F} onto its subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} singled out by the constraint g=0g=0. The usual equivalence group of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} was found in [1, 2]. We can easily prove this result using the classifying equations (10)–(12).

Proposition 4.

The usual equivalence group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} consists of the point transformations in the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f)(t,x,u,u_{x},f), whose components are of the form

t~=T1​t+T0,x~=X1​x+X2​u+X0,u~=U1​x+U2​u+U0,u~x~=U1+U2​uxX1+X2​ux,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=T_{1}t+T_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=X_{1}x+X_{2}u+X_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=U_{1}x+U_{2}u+U_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{U_{1}+U_{2}u_{x}}{X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x}},
f~=(X1+X2​ux)2T1​f,\displaystyle\tilde{f}=\frac{(X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x})^{2}}{T_{1}}f,

where TT’s, XX’s and UU’s are arbitrary constants with T1​(X1​U2−X2​U1)≠0T_{1}(X_{1}U_{2}-X_{2}U_{1})\neq 0.

Proof.

Restricted to the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} by the substitution g=0g=0 and g~=0\tilde{g}=0, the determining equation (9) itself becomes classifying for admissible transformations in this subclass. Therefore, it replaces its differential consequences, including the equations (11) and (12). The splitting of the equations (9) and (10) with respect f~\tilde{f} and f~u~x~\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} merely implies the equations

Vz=0,(Tt(Dx​X)2)z=0,z∈{t,x,u},Ut​Dx​X−Xt​Dx​U=0,\displaystyle V_{z}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\left(\frac{T_{t}}{(\mathrm{D}_{x}X)^{2}}\right)_{z}=0,\hskip 10.00002ptz\in\{t,x,u\},\hskip 10.00002ptU_{t}\mathrm{D}_{x}X-X_{t}\mathrm{D}_{x}U=0, (15)

which can be further split with respect to uxu_{x}. The second and the first equations of (15) with z∈{x,u}z\in\{x,u\} successively imply the equations Xx​x=Xu​x=Xu​u=0X_{xx}=X_{ux}=X_{uu}=0 and Ux​x=Uu​x=Uu​u=0U_{xx}=U_{ux}=U_{uu}=0. The last equation of (15) splits into the system Xz​Ut−Uz​Xt=0X_{z}U_{t}-U_{z}X_{t}=0 with z∈{x,u}z\in\{x,u\}, which has, as a homogeneous nondegenerate linear system of algebraic equations with respect to (Xt,Ut)(X_{t},U_{t}), the zero solution only, i.e., Xt=Ut=0X_{t}=U_{t}=0. Then the second equation with z=tz=t is equivalent to Tt​t=0T_{tt}=0. The derived equations exhaustively define the (t,x,u)(t,x,u)-components of equivalence transformations of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. In view of Remark 1, this completes the proof. ∎

The group Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} is a nontrivial conditional usual equivalence group of both the classes ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℱ\mathcal{F} under the condition g=0g=0. Elements of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}} with X2≠0X_{2}\neq 0 have no counterparts in Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} and Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and hence they are purely conditional equivalence transformations for the classes ℛ\mathcal{R} and ℱ\mathcal{F} under the condition g=0g=0.

The subgroup of Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} preserving the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} of ℱ\mathcal{F} is associated with constraint U3=0U_{3}=0, and the projection to the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f)(t,x,u,u_{x},f) maps this subgroup to a proper subgroup of Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}. This is why the group classification of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} up to Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalence does not reduce to the group classification of the class ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} up to Gℱ′∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}-equivalence under the above map of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} onto its subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. To make the group classifications of the classes ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} consistent, we should consider the stronger equivalence in the class ℱ\mathcal{F} that is associated with generalized equivalence group of this class.

Proposition 5.

The generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is constituted by the point transformations in the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g), whose components are of the form

t~=T¯1​t+T¯0,x~=X¯1​x+X¯2​u−g​X¯2​t+X¯0,u~=U¯1​x+U¯2​u+(T¯1​F¯−g​U¯2)​t+U¯0,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=\bar{T}^{1}t+\bar{T}^{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=\bar{X}^{1}x+\bar{X}^{2}u-g\bar{X}^{2}t+\bar{X}^{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=\bar{U}^{1}x+\bar{U}^{2}u+(\bar{T}^{1}\bar{F}-g\bar{U}^{2})t+\bar{U}^{0},
u~x~=U¯1+U¯2​uxX¯1+X¯2​ux,f~=(X¯1+X¯2​ux)2T¯1​f,g~=F¯,\displaystyle\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{\bar{U}^{1}+\bar{U}^{2}u_{x}}{\bar{X}^{1}+\bar{X}^{2}u_{x}},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{f}=\frac{(\bar{X}^{1}+\bar{X}^{2}u_{x})^{2}}{\bar{T}^{1}}f,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{g}=\bar{F},

where T¯\bar{T}’s, X¯\bar{X}’s, U¯\bar{U}’s and F¯\bar{F} are arbitrary smooth functions of gg with T¯1​(X¯1​U¯2−X¯2​U¯1)​F¯g≠0\bar{T}^{1}(\bar{X}^{1}\bar{U}^{2}-\bar{X}^{2}\bar{U}^{1})\bar{F}_{g}\neq 0.

Proof.

By the definition of generalized equivalence transformations [20, 21, 28, 39], their tt-, xx- and uu-components may in general depend on arbitrary elements. At the same time, these components of transformations from G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} can depend only on gg by the following reasons. The arbitrary element ff depends on uxu_{x}. Each generalized equivalence transformation generates a family of admissible transformations parameterized by the arbitrary elements [28]. Each contact admissible transformation in the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is the prolongation of a point admissible transformation to the first-order derivatives of uu, i.e., the class ℱ\mathcal{F} possesses no nontrivial contact admissible transformations.

We follow the proof of Proposition 3 but, due to potential dependence of the tt-, xx- and uu-components of generalized equivalence transformations on gg, here we cannot split with respect to this arbitrary element. This is the only essential difference with the proof of Proposition 3. Similarly to the proof of Proposition 4, the splitting of the equation (10) with respect f~\tilde{f} and f~u~x~\tilde{f}_{\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}} merely implies the equations

Vz=0,(Tt(Dx​X)2)z=0,z∈{t,x,u}.\displaystyle V_{z}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\left(\frac{T_{t}}{(\mathrm{D}_{x}X)^{2}}\right)_{z}=0,\hskip 10.00002ptz\in\{t,x,u\}. (16)

The further splitting of the second and the first equations of (16) with z∈{x,u}z\in\{x,u\} with respect to uxu_{x} successively yields the equations Xx​x=Xu​x=Xu​u=0X_{xx}=X_{ux}=X_{uu}=0 and Ux​x=Uu​x=Uu​u=0U_{xx}=U_{ux}=U_{uu}=0. Thus, Δx=Δu=0\Delta_{x}=\Delta_{u}=0. Then the equation (9) reduces to g​Δ+Ut​Dx​X−Xt​Dx​U=g~​Tt​Dx​Xg\Delta+U_{t}\mathrm{D}_{x}X-X_{t}\mathrm{D}_{x}U=\tilde{g}T_{t}\mathrm{D}_{x}X. Differentiating it with respect to xx and uu and splitting with respect to uxu_{x}, we obtain two systems, Xz​Ux​t−Uz​Xx​t=0X_{z}U_{xt}-U_{z}X_{xt}=0 and Xz​Uu​t−Uz​Xu​t=0X_{z}U_{ut}-U_{z}X_{ut}=0, where z∈{x,u}z\in\{x,u\}, which are equivalent, in view of the condition Δ≠0\Delta\neq 0, to the equations Xx​t=Ux​t=0X_{xt}=U_{xt}=0 and Xu​t=Uu​t=0X_{ut}=U_{ut}=0, respectively. Hence Δt=0\Delta_{t}=0, and differentiating the equation (9) with respect to tt gives Xz​Ut​t−Uz​Xt​t=0X_{z}U_{tt}-U_{z}X_{tt}=0 with z∈{x,u}z\in\{x,u\}, i.e., we also have Xt​t=Ut​t=0X_{tt}=U_{tt}=0. Taking into account the derived equations Xx​t=Xu​t=0X_{xt}=X_{ut}=0 in the second equation of (16) with z=tz=t immediately gives Tt​t=0T_{tt}=0.

In view of the constructed equations for admissible transformations, the (t,x,u)(t,x,u)-components of generalized equivalence transformations within the class ℱ\mathcal{F} should be of the form

t~=T¯1​t+T¯0,x~=X¯1​x+X¯2​u+X¯3​t+X¯0,u~=U¯1​x+U¯2​u+U¯3​t+U¯0,\tilde{t}=\bar{T}^{1}t+\bar{T}^{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=\bar{X}^{1}x+\bar{X}^{2}u+\bar{X}^{3}t+\bar{X}^{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}=\bar{U}^{1}x+\bar{U}^{2}u+\bar{U}^{3}t+\bar{U}^{0},

where T¯\bar{T}’s, X¯\bar{X}’s and U¯\bar{U}’s are smooth functions of gg with T¯1≠0\bar{T}^{1}\neq 0 and X¯1​U¯2−X¯2​U¯1=Δ≠0\bar{X}^{1}\bar{U}^{2}-\bar{X}^{2}\bar{U}^{1}=\Delta\neq 0. We represent the result of the splitting of the equation (9) with respect to uxu_{x} as the system

X¯1​U¯3−U¯1​X¯3=X¯1​Tt​g~−g​Δ,X¯2​U¯3−U¯2​X¯3=X¯2​Tt​g~.\displaystyle\bar{X}^{1}\bar{U}^{3}-\bar{U}^{1}\bar{X}^{3}=\bar{X}^{1}T_{t}\tilde{g}-g\Delta,\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{X}^{2}\bar{U}^{3}-\bar{U}^{2}\bar{X}^{3}=\bar{X}^{2}T_{t}\tilde{g}. (17)

It is clear from this system that the gg-component of any generalized equivalence transformation within the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is a function F¯\bar{F} of gg only, and we can choose this function as a parameter function merely constrained by the inequality F¯g≠0\bar{F}_{g}\neq 0, which is needed for the transformation nondegeneracy. Then the system (17) considered as a linear system of algebraic equations with respect to (X¯3,U¯3)(\bar{X}^{3},\bar{U}^{3}) possesses a unique solution resulting in the form of transformations from proposition’s statement. ∎

The usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is a (finite-dimensional) subgroup of the generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} that is singled out from G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} by the following system of constraints for the group parameters:

T¯g0=T¯g1=0,X¯g0=X¯g1=0,X¯2=0,U¯g0=U¯g1=U¯g2=0,T¯1​F¯g=U¯2.\bar{T}^{0}_{g}=\bar{T}^{1}_{g}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{X}^{0}_{g}=\bar{X}^{1}_{g}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{X}^{2}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{U}^{0}_{g}=\bar{U}^{1}_{g}=\bar{U}^{2}_{g}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\bar{T}^{1}\bar{F}_{g}=\bar{U}^{2}.

Denote by 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} the equivalence groupoid of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} and by 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} the subgroupoid of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} generated by the generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. The subgroupoid of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} generated by the usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is a proper subgroupoid of 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. Hence the group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is an example of a nontrivial generalized equivalence group, and it is also a nontrivial conditional generalized equivalence group of the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, where the specializing attribute “nontrivial” is related to both the attributes “conditional” and “generalized”. The dependence of group parameters on gg is needless for generating admissible transformations in the class ℱ\mathcal{F} and is merely a manifestation of the fact that the arbitrary element gg is constant within the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}. This is why we need to consider an effective generalized equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, which is a minimal subgroup of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} generating the subgroupoid 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. See [28] for related definitions. The only dependence on gg that is essential for generalized equivalence is the explicit involvement of gg in the tt-coefficient of the xx-component. At the same time, setting the group parameters T¯\bar{T}’s, X¯\bar{X}’s, U¯\bar{U}’s and T¯1​F¯−U¯2\bar{T}^{1}\bar{F}-\bar{U}^{2} to be constants singles out the subset of elements from G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} that is not a subgroup of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} although this subset is minimal among subsets of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} generating 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. The construction of an effective generalized equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is in fact more tricky.

Proposition 6.

An effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} is constituted by the point transformations

t~=T1​t+T0,x~=X1​x+X2​u−X2​g​t+X0,\displaystyle\tilde{t}=T_{1}t+T_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{x}=X_{1}x+X_{2}u-X_{2}gt+X_{0},
u~=U1​x+U2​u+(1−U2)​g​t+U3​t+T0T1​g+U0,u~x~=U1+U2​uxX1+X2​ux,\displaystyle\tilde{u}=U_{1}x+U_{2}u+(1-U_{2})gt+U_{3}t+\frac{T_{0}}{T_{1}}g+U_{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{U_{1}+U_{2}u_{x}}{X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x}},
f~=(X1+X2​ux)2T1​f,g~=g+U3T1,\displaystyle\tilde{f}=\frac{(X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x})^{2}}{T_{1}}f,\hskip 10.00002pt\tilde{g}=\frac{g+U_{3}}{T_{1}},

where TT’s, XX’s and UU’s are arbitrary constants with T1​(X1​U2−X2​U1)≠0T_{1}(X_{1}U_{2}-X_{2}U_{1})\neq 0.

Proof.

Consider the set H1H_{1} of the point transformations in the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g), whose components are of the form

t~=T1​t+T0,x~=X1​x+X2​u+(A11​g+A10)​t+B11​g+B10,u~=U1​x+U2​u+(A21​g+A20)​t+B21​g+B20,u~x~=U1+U2​uxX1+X2​ux,f~=(X1+X2​ux)2T1f,g~=C1​g+C0T1,\displaystyle\begin{split}&\tilde{t}=T_{1}t+T_{0},\\ &\tilde{x}=X_{1}x+X_{2}u+(A_{11}g+A_{10})t+B_{11}g+B_{10},\\ &\tilde{u}=U_{1}x+U_{2}u+(A_{21}g+A_{20})t+B_{21}g+B_{20},\\ &\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}}=\frac{U_{1}+U_{2}u_{x}}{X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x}},\quad\tilde{f}=\frac{(X_{1}+X_{2}u_{x})^{2}}{T_{1}}f,\quad\tilde{g}=\frac{C_{1}g+C_{0}}{T_{1}},\end{split} (18)

where TT’s, XX’s, UU’s, AA’s, BB’s and CC’s are arbitrary constants with T1​(X1​U2−X2​U1)​C1≠0T_{1}(X_{1}U_{2}-X_{2}U_{1})C_{1}\neq 0. It is obvious that this set is closed with respect to the composition of transformations and taking the inverse, i.e., it is a (local) transformation group with dimH1=16\dim H_{1}=16. Then the intersection H0:=H1∩G¯ℱ∼H_{0}:=H_{1}\cap\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of H1H_{1} with G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which is singled out from H1H_{1} by the constraints A10=0A_{10}=0, A11=−X2A_{11}=-X_{2}, A20=C0A_{20}=C_{0} and A21=C1−U2A_{21}=C_{1}-U_{2}, is also a group, and dimH0=12\dim H_{0}=12. The subgroup H0H_{0} of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} generates the entire subgroupoid 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which is generated by G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. At the same time, for each fixed pair of the arbitrary elements (f,g)(f,g), the subgroupoid 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} contains a precisely nine-parameter family of admissible transformations with the source (f,g)(f,g). This is why we should try to find three more constraints for group parameters of the group H1H_{1} in order to construct a nine-dimensional subgroup of H0H_{0} that still generates the entire 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}.

We analyze the composition of two arbitrary elements from the group H0H_{0}, 𝒯^=𝒯~​𝒯\hat{\mathcal{T}}=\tilde{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{T} with 𝒯~,𝒯∈H0\tilde{\mathcal{T}},\mathcal{T}\in H_{0}. These generalized equivalence transformations have the general form (18), where group parameters satisfy the above constraints for the subgroup H0H_{0}. We additionally reparameterize H0H_{0} with replacing the parameter B21B_{21} by B21′+T0/T1B_{21}^{\prime}+T_{0}/T_{1} and mark the group-parameter values corresponding to 𝒯^\hat{\mathcal{T}} and 𝒯~\tilde{\mathcal{T}} by hats and tildes, respectively. We obtain, in particular, the following expressions for group-parameter values of the composition 𝒯^\hat{\mathcal{T}}:

C^1=C~1​C1,B^11=X~1​B11+X~2​B21′+B~11T1,B^21′=U~1​B11+U~2​B21′+B~21′T1,\displaystyle\hat{C}_{1}=\tilde{C}_{1}C_{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\hat{B}_{11}=\tilde{X}_{1}B_{11}+\tilde{X}_{2}B_{21}^{\prime}+\frac{\tilde{B}_{11}}{T_{1}},\hskip 10.00002pt\hat{B}_{21}^{\prime}=\tilde{U}_{1}B_{11}+\tilde{U}_{2}B_{21}^{\prime}+\frac{\tilde{B}_{21}^{\prime}}{T_{1}},

which imply that the constrains C1=1C_{1}=1, B11=B21′=0B_{11}=B_{21}^{\prime}=0 singling out G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} from the subgroup H0H_{0} are preserved by the composition of transformations and taking the inverse in H0H_{0}. Therefore, G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is really a group. It generates the entire subgroupoid 𝒮ℱ∼\mathcal{S}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, and any its proper subset does not possess this property, i.e., it is a minimal subgroup of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} with this property. ∎

The usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} is not contained in the effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} constructed in Proposition 6. The intersection Gℱ∼∩G^ℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}\cap\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is singled out from Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} by the constraints T0=0T_{0}=0 and U2=1U_{2}=1.

To prove an assertion generalizing the above claim, we need to consider the infinitesimal counterparts of related groups. For convenience, we introduce the following dual notation for relevant vector fields on the space with the coordinates (t,x,u,ux,f,g)(t,x,u,u_{x},f,g):

Q1=Pt=∂t,Q2=Dt=t∂t−f∂f−g∂g,\displaystyle Q^{1}=P^{t}=\partial_{t},\hskip 10.00002ptQ^{2}=D^{t}=t\partial_{t}-f\partial_{f}-g\partial_{g},

[Zt,Dt]=−Zt,[Zx,Dx]=−Zx,[Zt,Du]=Zt,[Zx,Du]=Zx,\displaystyle[Z^{t},D^{t}]=-Z^{t},\ [Z^{x},D^{x}]=-Z^{x},\ [Z^{t},D^{u}]=Z^{t},\ [Z^{x},D^{u}]=Z^{x},
[Pt,R]=−g​Px,[Pu,R]=Px,[Dx,R]=−R,[Du,R]=R,[Zx,R]=Dx−Du+g​Zt.\displaystyle[P^{t},R]=-gP^{x},\ [P^{u},R]=P^{x},\ [D^{x},R]=-R,\ [D^{u},R]=R,\ [Z^{x},R]=D^{x}-D^{u}+gZ^{t}.

The Lie algebras 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, 𝔤¯ℱ∼\bar{\mathfrak{g}}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and 𝔤^ℱ∼\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} are naturally called the usual equivalence algebra, the generalized equivalence algebra and an effective generalized equivalence algebra of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}, respectively. Each of them is merely the set of infinitesimal generators of one-parameter subgroups of the corresponding group. In order to construct all such generators, we successively take one of the group parameter in the respective general form of group elements to depend on a continuous subgroup parameter δ\delta and set the other parameter-functions to their values corresponding to the identity transformations, which are T1=X1=U2=1T_{1}=X_{1}=U_{2}=1 and T0=X0=X2=U0=U1=U3=0T_{0}=X_{0}=X_{2}=U_{0}=U_{1}=U_{3}=0 for the groups Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} (the parameter X2X_{2} is relevant only for G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}) and similarly T¯1=X¯1=U¯2=1\bar{T}^{1}=\bar{X}^{1}=\bar{U}^{2}=1, T¯0=X¯0=X¯2=U¯0=U¯1=0\bar{T}^{0}=\bar{X}^{0}=\bar{X}^{2}=\bar{U}^{0}=\bar{U}^{1}=0 and F¯=g\bar{F}=g for the group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}. Then we differentiate the transformation components with respect to δ\delta and evaluate the result at δ=0\delta=0. As a result, we derive that

𝔤^ℱ∼=⟨Pt+g​Pu,Dt,Px,Dx,Pu,Du−g​Zt,Zt,Zx,R⟩,\displaystyle\hat{\mathfrak{g}}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}=\langle P^{t}+gP^{u},\,D^{t},\,P^{x},\,D^{x},\,P^{u},\,D^{u}-gZ^{t},\,Z^{t},\,Z^{x},\,R\rangle,

where the coefficients ϑ\vartheta’s run through the set of smooth functions of gg, i.e., the algebra 𝔤¯ℱ∼\bar{\mathfrak{g}}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is the module over the ring of smooth functions of gg with basis (Q1,…,Q9)(Q^{1},\dots,Q^{9}) equipped with the Lie bracket of vector fields.

Theorem 7.

Any effective generalized equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} does not contain the usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of this class.

Proof.

We prove the following re-formulated assertion: Suppose that a subgroup of the generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} contains the usual equivalence group Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of this class and generates the same subgroupoid of the equivalence groupoid 𝒢ℱ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} as the entire group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} does. Then this subgroup is not an effective generalized equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F}.

A complete list of discrete usual equivalence transformations of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} that are independent up to combining with each other and with continuous usual equivalence transformations of this class is exhausted by the involutions ItI^{t}, IxI^{x} and IuI^{u} alternating the signs of (t,f,g)(t,f,g), (x,ux)(x,u_{x}) and (u,ux,g)(u,u_{x},g), respectively. Among generalized equivalence transformations, there is one more independent discrete transformation IgI^{g}: (t~,x~,u~,u~x~,f~,g~)=(t,x,u−2​g​t,ux,f,−g)(\tilde{t},\tilde{x},\tilde{u},\tilde{u}_{\tilde{x}},\tilde{f},\tilde{g})=(t,x,u-2gt,u_{x},f,-g). Discrete equivalence transformations play an auxiliary role in the course of the proof.

It suffices to prove the infinitesimal counterpart of the above assertion, which states the following. Let a subalgebra 𝔥\mathfrak{h} of 𝔤¯ℱ∼\bar{\mathfrak{g}}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} contain 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and a vector field Q=∑i=19ζi​QiQ=\sum_{i=1}^{9}\zeta^{i}Q^{i}, where ζi=ζi​(g)\zeta^{i}=\zeta^{i}(g) are smooth functions of gg with ζ9≠0\zeta^{9}\neq 0, be invariant with respect to discrete transformations in Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, I∗t​𝔥,I∗x​𝔥,I∗u​𝔥⊆𝔥I^{t}_{*}\mathfrak{h},I^{x}_{*}\mathfrak{h},I^{u}_{*}\mathfrak{h}\subseteq\mathfrak{h}, and be associated with a transformation (pseudo)group. Then this subalgebra properly contains another subalgebra 𝔰\mathfrak{s} among whose elements there are Kj=∑i=19χi​j​QiK^{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{9}\chi^{ij}Q^{i}, where χi​j\chi^{ij}, i,j=1,…,9i,j=1,\dots,9, are smooth functions of gg with det(χi​j)≠0\det(\chi^{ij})\neq 0, and which is also invariant with respect to I∗tI^{t}_{*}, I∗xI^{x}_{*} and I∗uI^{u}_{*} and is associated with a transformation (pseudo)group. If the algebra 𝔥\mathfrak{h} contains the pure vector field RR, then we commute RR with elements of 𝔤ℱ∼\mathfrak{g}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and successively obtain that

3 Classification of Lie symmetries

In order to compute the maximal Lie invariance algebras of equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, we employ the infinitesimal method [27, 31]. The infinitesimal generator of a one-parameter Lie-symmetry group of an equation from the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is a vector field Q=τ(t,x,u)∂t+ξ(t,x,u)∂x+η(t,x,u)∂uQ=\tau(t,x,u)\partial_{t}+\xi(t,x,u)\partial_{x}+\eta(t,x,u)\partial_{u} on the space with coordinates (t,x,u)(t,x,u) with the components τ\tau, ξ\xi and η\eta being the smooth functions of these coordinates. The infinitesimal invariance criterion requires that

Q(2)​(ut−f⁡(ux)​ux​x−g⁡(u))|ut=f⁡(ux)​ux​x+g⁡(u)=0,\displaystyle Q^{(2)}(u_{t}-f(u_{x})u_{xx}-g(u))\big|_{u_{t}=f(u_{x})u_{xx}+g(u)}=0, (19)

where Q(2)Q^{(2)} is the second prolongation of the vector field QQ defined by the well-known prolongation formula [27], Q(2)=Q+η(1,0)∂ut+η(0,1)∂ux+η(2,0)∂ut​t+η(1,1)∂ut​x+η(0,2)∂ux​x,Q^{(2)}=Q+\eta^{(1,0)}\partial_{u_{t}}+\eta^{(0,1)}\partial_{u_{x}}+\eta^{(2,0)}\partial_{u_{tt}}+\eta^{(1,1)}\partial_{u_{tx}}+\eta^{(0,2)}\partial_{u_{xx}}, with the coefficients η\eta’s defined as ηα=Dα​(η−τ​ut−ξ​ux)+τ​uα+δ1+ξ​uα+δ2.\eta^{\alpha}=\mathrm{D}^{\alpha}\left(\eta-\tau u_{t}-\xi u_{x}\right)+\tau u_{\alpha+\delta_{1}}+\xi u_{\alpha+\delta_{2}}. Here α=(α1,α2)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}) is a multi-index, Dα=Dtα1​Dxα2\mathrm{D}^{\alpha}=\mathrm{D}_{t}^{\alpha_{1}}\mathrm{D}_{x}^{\alpha_{2}}, Dt=∂t+∑αuα+δ1∂uα\mathrm{D}_{t}=\partial_{t}+\sum_{\alpha}u_{\alpha+\delta_{1}}\partial_{u_{\alpha}} and Dx=∂x+∑αuα+δ2∂uα\mathrm{D}_{x}=\partial_{x}+\sum_{\alpha}u_{\alpha+\delta_{2}}\partial_{u_{\alpha}} are the total derivative operators with respect to tt and xx, respectively, δ1=(1,0)\delta_{1}=(1,0) and δ2=(0,1)\delta_{2}=(0,1).

Since the class ℛ\mathcal{R} consists of evolution equations, the tt-component of QQ does not depend on xx and uu, i.e., τ=τ⁡(t)\tau=\tau(t) [18, 19].

We expand the expression in the left hand side of (19), substitute f⁡(ux)​ux​x+g⁡(u)f(u_{x})u_{xx}+g(u) for utu_{t} and then split the resulting equation with respect to ux​xu_{xx}. This gives the system of determining equations for the components of Lie-symmetry vector fields of equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R},

(−ξuux+2(ηu−ξx)ux+ηx)fux+(−2ξuux+τt−2ξx)f=0,\displaystyle\left(-\xi_{u}u_{x}{}^{\!2}+(\eta_{u}-\xi_{x})u_{x}+\eta_{x}\right)f_{u_{x}}+(-2\xi_{u}u_{x}+\tau_{t}-2\xi_{x})f=0, (20a)
(−ξu​uux3+(ηu​u−2ξx​u)ux2+(2ηx​u−ξx​x)ux+ηx​x)f+(ξt+ξug)ux+η​gu+(τt−ηu)​g−ηt=0.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\left(-\xi_{uu}u_{x}^{3}+(\eta_{uu}-2\xi_{xu})u_{x}{}^{\!2}+(2\eta_{xu}-\xi_{xx})u_{x}+\eta_{xx}\right)f+(\xi_{t}+\xi_{u}g)u_{x}\\ &\qquad{}+\eta g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta_{u})g-\eta_{t}=0.\end{split} (20b)

Thus, the problem of group classification for the class ℛ\mathcal{R} reduces to the classification of solutions of the system (20), depending on values of the arbitrary elements ff and gg up to Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence or up to the general point equivalence.

To find the kernel Lie invariance algebras of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and of its subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L}, ℱ\mathcal{F}, ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} (each of these algebras is the intersection of the maximal Lie invariance algebras of equations from the corresponding (sub)class), we successively split the equations (20a) and (20b) with respect to the arbitrary elements and their derivatives and with respect to uxu_{x}, taking into account the associated auxiliary equations for arbitrary elements. See also the papers [8], [10] and [1, 2] for the kernel Lie invariance algebras of the classes ℛ\mathcal{R}, ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, respectively.

Proposition 8.

The kernel Lie invariance algebra 𝔤ℛ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{R}} of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} coincides with the kernel Lie invariance algebras 𝔤ℋ∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{H}} and 𝔤𝒞∩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{C}} of its subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒞\mathcal{C}, and it is spanned by the vector fields ∂t\partial_{t} and ∂x\partial_{x},

𝔤ℛ∩=𝔤ℋ∩=𝔤𝒞∩=⟨∂t,∂x⟩.\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{H}}=\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{C}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x}\rangle.

The kernel Lie invariance algebras of the subclasses ℒ\mathcal{L}, ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} are respectively

𝔤ℒ∩=⟨∂t,∂x,x∂x⟩,𝔤ℱ∩=⟨∂t,∂x,∂u⟩,𝔤ℱ′∩=⟨∂t,∂x,∂u, 2t∂t+x∂x+u∂u⟩.\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{L}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x},\,x\partial_{x}\rangle,\hskip 10.00002pt\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x},\partial_{u}\rangle,\hskip 10.00002pt\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x},\,\partial_{u},\,2t\partial_{t}+x\partial_{x}+u\partial_{u}\rangle.

Accurately merging the group classifications of the subclasses 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℒ\mathcal{L} that is presented in Lemma 14 below, that were carried out in [1, 2] and in [10], and that can be obtained by mapping with the hodograph transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=u\tilde{x}=u, u~=x\tilde{u}=x from the group classification of the class of Kolmogorov equations given in [40], respectively, we get the following assertion.

Theorem 9.

A complete list of inequivalent Lie-symmetry extensions in the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is exhausted by the cases given in Table 1, where we use Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-, G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-, Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}- and 𝒢ℒ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{L}}-equivalence for equations from the subclasses 𝒞\mathcal{C}, ℱ\mathcal{F}, ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℒ\mathcal{L}, respectively.

Here 𝒢ℒ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{L}} denotes the equivalence groupoid of the class ℒ\mathcal{L}.

Notation for Table 1. Numbers with the same Arabic numerals and different Roman letters correspond to cases that are equivalent with respect to additional equivalence transformations. Explicit formulas for these transformations are presented in the footnote of Table 1. The cases that are numbered with different numbers in Arabic numerals are reciprocally inequivalent with respect to point transformations. Lie invariance algebras presented in Cases 1, 1 and 1 are maximal only if the corresponding tuples of the arbitrary elements (f,g)(f,g) are Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent to those from other cases.

The (usual) equivalence groups of the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} coincide with each other and with the group Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}. This is why within the class ℛ\mathcal{R}, Cases 1′ and 1a′ can be attached to Cases 1 and 1a by allowing the value n=0n=0 in the latter cases.

Crossing out the numbers of Cases 1c and 1d indicates that they are implicitly presented in the course of listing Lie-symmetry extensions for the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} since both of them are G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}-equivalent to Case 1a.

Remark 10.

We should carefully treat arguments of logarithm and bases of powers with noninteger exponents. The condition of positivity is justified for uu by physical arguments but this is not the case for uxu_{x}. Moreover, assuming uu positive makes impossible the change of the sign of uu, which results in the disappearance of some discrete equivalence transformations. This is why we use the absolute values of uu, uxu_{x} and similar expressions as arguments of logarithm and as bases of related powers with general real exponents. This is not necessary for some particular exponents (more specifically, integer exponents and rational exponents with odd denominators) but replacing an absolute value by the value itself in a power base may lead to modifying the gauging of the coefficient of this power since such a replacement may affect the action of discrete equivalence transformations on power coefficients.

Remark 11.

To construct an exhaustive list of Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent Lie-symmetry extensions for the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}, we should extend Cases 1–1 using transformations from the generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of ℱ\mathcal{F} (or, equivalently, from the effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, which is more convenient) and then gauge arising parameters by elements of Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}. In each of the Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent cases constructed, we can set g∈{0,1}modGℛ∼g\in\{0,1\}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}, and a complete list of Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent values of the arbitrary element ff is exhausted by the general value (the extended Case 1) and

|ux+δ|n,|ux+μ|n|ux+ν|n+2;eux,e(ux+λ)−1(ux+λ)2;em​arctan⁡(ux+λ)(ux+λ)2+1;1,(ux+δ)−2.|u_{x}+\delta|^{n},\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{|u_{x}+\mu|^{n}}{|u_{x}+\nu|^{n+2}};\hskip 10.00002pte^{u_{x}},\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{e^{(u_{x}+\lambda)^{-1}}}{(u_{x}+\lambda)^{2}};\hskip 10.00002pt\frac{e^{m\arctan(u_{x}+\lambda)}}{(u_{x}+\lambda)^{2}+1};\hskip 10.00002pt1,\hskip 10.00002pt(u_{x}+\delta)^{-2}.

Here n∈ℝ∖{0,−2}n\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0,-2\}, δ∈{0,1}modGℛ∼\delta\in\{0,1\}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}, λ,μ,ν,m∈ℝ\lambda,\mu,\nu,m\in\mathbb{R}, μ≠ν\mu\neq\nu, and one nonzero constant among μ\mu and ν\nu can be set to be equal 11 modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence, m⩾0modGℛ∼m\geqslant 0\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}. Semicolons in the above displayed equation separate the extensions of Cases 1, 1, 1 and 1, respectively. In the course of implementing the above procedure for Case 1, we should take into account the formula for sum of arctangents,

arctan⁡y+arctan⁡z={arctan⁡y+z1−y​z+π2​(sgny)​(1+sgn(1−y​z)),ify​z≠1,π2​sgny,ify​z=1.\displaystyle\arctan y+\arctan z=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\arctan\dfrac{y+z}{1-yz}+\dfrac{\pi}{2}(\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits y)(1+\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits(1-yz)),&\mbox{if}\quad yz\neq 1,\\ \dfrac{\pi}{2}\mathop{\rm sgn}\nolimits y,&\mbox{if}\quad yz=1.\end{array}\right.
Remark 12.

Recall that the class ℒ\mathcal{L} is similar to the class 𝒦\mathcal{K} of Kolmogorov equations of the general form (3) with respect to a point transformation, which is the hodograph transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=u\tilde{x}=u, u~=x\tilde{u}=x. This is why the groups classifications of the class ℒ\mathcal{L} up to 𝒢ℒ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{L}}- and Gℒ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{L}}-equivalences reduce to their counterparts for the class 𝒦\mathcal{K}; see the theoretical background on mappings between classes of differential equations that are generated by point transformations in [47]. For the part of Table 1 related to the class ℒ\mathcal{L}, we use a complete list of inequivalent (up to general point equivalence) Lie-symmetry extensions that is constructed for the general class of (1+1)-dimensional Kolmogorov equations in [40, Corollary 7] and coincides with such a list for the class 𝒦\mathcal{K}. The reason for this is that a similar list for the group classification of the class 𝒦\mathcal{K} up to the equivalence generated by its equivalence group is too cumbersome [29].

Theorem 13.

A complete list of 𝒢ℛ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent (i.e., inequivalent up point transformations) cases of Lie-symmetry extensions in the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is exhausted by Cases 1, 1, 1∪{}\cup{}1′, 1a∪{}\cup{}1a′, 1, 1a, 1, 1, 1a, 1, 1, 1a, and 1–1 of Table 1.
