4 Method of furcate splitting

Although the literature dedicated to group classification of classes (of systems) of differential equations is vast, a considerable part thereof is not trustworthy at all. The main problem lies in the fact that often a brute-force approach is applied to tackle group classification problems. Albeit this approach is definitely applicable (but certainly inefficient) for some simple classes of differential equations, it requires a very thorough inspection to keep track of various cases that arise upon integrating the corresponding determining equations for Lie symmetries, otherwise it leads to missed, overlapping, repeated and/or incorrect classification cases. These flaws happened in the majority of papers where the brute-force approach is used for group classification of differential equations. Moreover, since this approach is often cumbersome, such papers do not contain details of solutions, which makes pretty hard to find flaws in the computations afterwards.

While the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} does not possess a necessary structure to employ the powerful algebraic method of group classification, a brute force is still not the last resort. The best choice here is the method of furcate splitting. This method was suggested and applied for the first time in [26] but its name appeared later in [17]. See also examples of its application in [37, 46, 48, 49]. It is basically a refinement of the direct approach to group classification. In contrast to the chaotical integration of the classifying equations and the irregular selection of cases with Lie-symmetry extensions within the framework of the direct approach, the method of furcate splitting provides an algorithm for systematically finding such cases. It is worth to note that the method is effective for classes with arbitrary elements depending on a few arguments. So far, it was used for classes with arbitrary elements depending on at most two arguments [26]. This limit for manually using the method seems to be reasonable in view of the necessity of verifying the compatibility condition of arising equations, which becomes the more difficult problem the more arguments the arbitrary elements depend on.

The method of furcate splitting can be easily understood by examples but the description of its standard version in the general setting is quite tedious, not to mention its various modifications. Nevertheless, below we present this description, and in Section 5 we illustrate possible complications for using the method if arbitrary elements of the class under study depend on different arguments, which is the case for the class ℛ\mathcal{R}; see also the related discussion in the end of Section 7.

Consider a class of (systems of) differential equations

ℒ|𝒮={ℒθ:L(x,u(r),θ(x,u(r)))=0∣θ∈𝒮}.\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}}=\{\mathscr{L}_{\theta}\colon L(x,u_{(r)},\theta(x,u_{(r)}))=0\mid\theta\in\mathscr{S}\}.

Here and below in this section the notation differs from the other sections of the paper: xx and uu are the tuples of independent and dependent variables, respectively, constituting the coordinates for a coordinate space, u(r)u_{(r)} denotes the tuple of derivatives of uu with respect to xx up to order rr, which also includes the uu’s as the derivatives of order zero, and LL is a tuple of differential functions in uu, parameterized by the tuple of functions θ=(θ1​(x,u(r)),…,θp​(x,u(r)))\theta=(\theta^{1}(x,u_{(r)}),\dots,\theta^{p}(x,u_{(r)})), called the arbitrary elements of the class ℒ|𝒮\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}}. The arbitrary-element tuple runs through the solution set 𝒮\mathscr{S} of an auxiliary system AS{\rm AS} of differential equations and inequalities in θ\theta, S⁡(x,u(r),θ(q)​(x,u(r)))=0S(x,u_{(r)},\theta_{(q)}(x,u_{(r)}))=0 and, e.g., Σ⁡(x,u(r),θ(q)​(x,u(r)))≠0\Sigma(x,u_{(r)},\theta_{(q)}(x,u_{(r)}))\neq 0, where (x,u(r))(x,u_{(r)}) is assumed to be the tuple of independent variables, and the notation θ(q)\theta_{(q)} encompasses the partial derivatives of the arbitrary elements θ\theta up to order qq with respect to both xx and u(r)u_{(r)}. See [35, 39] for more detailed explanations on the notion of class of differential equations.

Denote by 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} the maximal Lie invariance algebra of a system ℒθ∈ℒ|𝒮\mathscr{L}_{\theta}\in\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}}. The system of determining equations DE⁡[θ]{\rm DE}[\theta] for components of vector fields in 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} may split into two subsystems. The equations of one of these subsystems, CE⁡[θ]{\rm CE}[\theta], essentially involve arbitrary elements and are called classifying equations, and the other subsystem, SE{\rm SE}, does not involve θ\theta and is thus shared by all ℒθ∈ℒ|𝒮\mathscr{L}_{\theta}\in\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}}. The subsystem SE{\rm SE} can be integrated directly, thus specifying the general form of Lie-symmetry vector fields of systems in ℒ|𝒮\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}}. The subsystem CE⁡[θ]{\rm CE}[\theta] with a fixed value of the arbitrary-element tuple θ\theta is the system of specific equations for the components of vector fields in 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta}. The solution set of the joint system DE⁡[θ]{\rm DE}[\theta] is a linear space in view of the fact that DE⁡[θ]{\rm DE}[\theta] is a homogeneous linear system of differential equations with respect to the components of Lie-symmetry vector fields. Conversely, fixing a vector field QQ on the space with coordinate (x,u)(x,u), we obtain a system of differential equations for the values of θ\theta for which the corresponding system ℒθ\mathscr{L}_{\theta} admits QQ as a Lie-symmetry vector field.

The system AS{\rm AS} as a rule includes equations implying the independence of θ\theta on certain independent or dependent variables or, more generally, on certain functional combinations of these variables. It is convenient to replace the coordinates (x,u(r))(x,u_{(r)}) in the rrth order jet space by the (local-)coordinate tuple zz that is split into two subtuples, z^\hat{z} and zˇ\check{z}, such that z^\hat{z} is a maximal tuple of coordinates not involved in θ\theta, and each of the tuples z^\hat{z} and zˇ\check{z} is split into two subtuples, z^′\hat{z}^{\prime}, z^′′\hat{z}^{\prime\prime} and zˇ′\check{z}^{\prime}, zˇ′′\check{z}^{\prime\prime}, where z^′\hat{z}^{\prime} and zˇ′\check{z}^{\prime} are maximal subtuples of z^\hat{z} and zˇ\check{z}, respectively, that appear in arguments of functions parameterizing the general solution of SE{\rm SE}. We choose the tuple z˘′\breve{z}^{\prime} of functions of (x,u)(x,u) such that the joint tuple (z^′,zˇ′,z˘′)(\hat{z}^{\prime},\check{z}^{\prime},\breve{z}^{\prime}) gives new coordinates in the space of (x,u)(x,u). In most of practical computations by the method of furcate splitting, the optimal choice of z^′\hat{z}^{\prime}, z^′′\hat{z}^{\prime\prime}, zˇ′\check{z}^{\prime}, zˇ′′\check{z}^{\prime\prime} and z˘′\breve{z}^{\prime} is obvious, cf. Section 5.

We substitute the expressions for the components of Lie-symmetry vector fields that are specified by SE{\rm SE} into CE⁡[θ]{\rm CE}[\theta] and split the obtained system with respect to z^′′\hat{z}^{\prime\prime}. This leads to the system CE′​[θ]{\rm CE}^{\prime}[\theta] for the constants and functions parameterizing these expressions, which is supposed to be of the form

∑i=is−1+1isψiFi=0,s=1,…,|CE′|,\sum_{i=i_{s-1}+1}^{i_{s}}\psi^{i}F^{i}=0,\hskip 10.00002pts=1,\dots,|{\rm CE}^{\prime}|,

where 0=i0<i1<⋯<i|CE′|=N0=i_{0}<i_{1}<\dots<i_{|{\rm CE}^{\prime}|}=N with N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, and |CE′||{\rm CE}^{\prime}| denotes the number of (independent) equations in CE′​[θ]{\rm CE}^{\prime}[\theta]. The functions FiF^{i}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, are known differential functions of θ\theta with zˇ\check{z} assumed to be the tuple of independent variables. The coefficients ψi\psi^{i}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, may depend on (z^′,zˇ′,z˘′)(\hat{z}^{\prime},\check{z}^{\prime},\breve{z}^{\prime}) and are in fact parameterized by an element of 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta}.

Let us imagine that the algebra 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} is known for each fixed θ\theta. Substituting values of the above parameters corresponding to a vector field in 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} and of the variables z^′\hat{z}^{\prime} into the system CE′​[θ]{\rm CE}^{\prime}[\theta] and varying the vector field within 𝔤θ\mathfrak{g}_{\theta} and the variables z^′\hat{z}^{\prime} give a family (denoted by TFF{\rm TFF}) of systems for θ\theta of the same general form called the template form,

∑i=is−1+1isaiFi=0,s=1,…,|CE′|,\sum_{i=i_{s-1}+1}^{i_{s}}a^{i}F^{i}=0,\hskip 10.00002pts=1,\dots,|{\rm CE}^{\prime}|,

where coefficients aia^{i}, i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, may depend on (zˇ′,z˘′)(\check{z}^{\prime},\breve{z}^{\prime}). In general, these coefficients are not precisely known at this stage but they may satisfy known constraints.

Let kk be the maximal number of systems in TFF{\rm TFF} such that the rank of the collection of the coefficient tuples a¯q=(aq​1,…,aq​N)\bar{a}^{q}=(a^{q1},\dots,a^{qN}) of these systems equals their number, rankA=k\mathop{\rm rank}A=k with A:=(aq​i)q=1,…,ki=1,…,NA:=(a^{qi})_{q=1,\dots,k}^{i=1,\dots,N}. It is obvious that 0⩽k⩽N0\leqslant k\leqslant N. The condition of consistency of systems within TFF{\rm TFF} and of these systems with AS{\rm AS} additionally majorizes the possible values of kk.

Supposing a certain value for kk within the range of possible values of kk, we study the consistency of TFF{\rm TFF}. The consideration can be partitioned into cases by choosing a sequence of k×kk\times k minors of the matrix AA in a way consistent with the relevant equivalence within the class ℒ|𝒮\mathscr{L}|_{\mathscr{S}} and by successively supposing that a minor in the sequence does not vanish and all the preceding minors are zero. Some of the coefficients aq​ia^{qi} can be gauged using equivalence transformations in view of the made supposition or derived constraints at this or further steps. For each of the cases, one should

  • •

    derive the conditions implied by the consistency of TFF{\rm TFF} on the coefficients aq​ia^{qi} and additionally gauge these coefficients by equivalence transformations (if possible),

  • •

    split the system CE′​[θ]{\rm CE}^{\prime}[\theta] on the solution set of the joint system of AS{\rm AS} and TFF{\rm TFF} with respect to parametric derivatives of θ\theta,

  • •

    solve the obtained system of additional determining equations for still unspecified parameters in Lie symmetry vector fields,

  • •

    derive the precise form of TFF{\rm TFF} for the computed algebra of vector fields and check its consistency with the supposed value of kk and other suppositions,

  • •

    if the consistency holds, solve the specified system TFF{\rm TFF} with respect to θ\theta.

One has k=0k=0 if and only if the classifying equations are identically satisfied in view of SE{\rm SE}, which corresponds to the general case without Lie-symmetry extension.

The value k=1k=1 is associated with minimal Lie-symmetry extensions. For this value of kk, the second step of the above procedure is convenient to be carried out in a special way since it means that the tuple ψ¯=(ψ1,…,ψN)\bar{\psi}=(\psi^{1},\dots,\psi^{N}) is proportional to a¯1\bar{a}^{1}, ψi=λ​a1​i\psi^{i}=\lambda a^{1i}. Here the multiplier λ\lambda may depend on (z^′,zˇ′,z˘′)(\hat{z}^{\prime},\check{z}^{\prime},\breve{z}^{\prime}) or, equivalently, on (x,u)(x,u), and this dependence can be easily specified in view of the form of ψ¯\bar{\psi} and a¯1\bar{a}^{1}.

5 Solution of group classification problem for regular subclass

In this section we prove the following assertion.

Proposition 14.

A complete list of Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent Lie-symmetry extensions in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} is exhausted by Cases 1, 1, 1, 1a, 1b, 1, 1a, 1b, 1c, 1 and 1b of Table 1.

Recall that the G𝒞∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{C}}-equivalence coincides with the restriction of the Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalence to the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}.

It turns out that additionally to τx=τu=0\tau_{x}=\tau_{u}=0, components of Lie-symmetry vector fields of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} satisfy more determining equations not involving the arbitrary elements ff and gg.

Lemma 15.

Under the conditions fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0, (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 and gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0, the system (20) implies

ξx​x=ξx​u=ξu​u=ηx​x=ηx​u=ηu​u=0.\displaystyle\xi_{xx}=\xi_{xu}=\xi_{uu}=\eta_{xx}=\eta_{xu}=\eta_{uu}=0. (21)
Proof.

We consider two obvious differential consequences of the system (20). One of the consequences is derived by acting the operators ux∂u+∂xu_{x}\partial_{u}+\partial_{x} and −∂ux{}-\partial_{u_{x}} on the equations (20a) and (20b), respectively, and summing the obtained equations, which gives

(ξu​uux−22ηu​uux−2ηx​u−ξx​x)f=ξt+ξug.\displaystyle\big(\xi_{uu}u_{x}{}^{\!2}-2\eta_{uu}u_{x}-2\eta_{xu}-\xi_{xx}\big)f=\xi_{t}+\xi_{u}g. (22)

The other consequence is the sum of the equation (20b) with the equation (22) multiplied by uxu_{x},

((ηu​u+2ξx​u)ux+22ξx​xux−ηx​x)f=ηgu+(τt−ηu)g−ηt.\displaystyle\big((\eta_{uu}+2\xi_{xu})u_{x}{}^{\!2}+2\xi_{xx}u_{x}-\eta_{xx}\big)f=\eta g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta_{u})g-\eta_{t}. (23)

The equations (22) and (23) hint that the proof is partitioned into three cases, depending on whether these equations imply conditions on ff and what structures of such conditions are,

1.(1/f)ux​ux​ux≠0,2.(1/f)ux​ux​ux=0,(1/f)ux​ux≠0,and3.(1/f)ux​ux=0.1.\ (1/f)_{u_{x}u_{x}u_{x}}\neq 0,\hskip 10.00002pt2.\ (1/f)_{u_{x}u_{x}u_{x}}=0,\ (1/f)_{u_{x}u_{x}}\neq 0,\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt3.\ (1/f)_{u_{x}u_{x}}=0.

In the first case, we can split the above differential consequences with respect to both ff and uxu_{x}, which directly leads to the required equations.

The third condition means that f=(ux+γ)−1modGℛ∼f=(u_{x}+\gamma)^{-1}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}. (Recall that we suppose the inequality fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0.) Substituting the expression for ff into (20a) and splitting with respect to uxu_{x} give the equations ξu=0\xi_{u}=0, ηu=γ⁡(τt−ξx)\eta_{u}=\gamma(\tau_{t}-\xi_{x}) and ηx=τt−ξx\eta_{x}=\tau_{t}-\xi_{x}, which imply ηx​u=ηu​u=0\eta_{xu}=\eta_{uu}=0. Using derived equations, we simplify the equation (22) and then treat it in the same way, which in particular gives ξx​x=0\xi_{xx}=0, and thus also ηx​x=0\eta_{xx}=0.

In the second case, which is much more complicated than the other cases, modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence we can set f=(ux+22βux+γ)−1f=(u_{x}{}^{\!2}+2\beta u_{x}+\gamma)^{-1}, where (β,γ)≠(0,0)(\beta,\gamma)\neq(0,0) since (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0. Substituting the expression for ff into (20a), splitting with respect to uxu_{x} and arranging the obtained equations, we get

ηu=−β​ξu+12​τt,ηx=−β​ξx+β2​τt+(β2−γ)​ξu,(β2−γ)​(2​ξx−β​ξu−τt)=0.\displaystyle\eta_{u}=-\beta\xi_{u}+\frac{1}{2}\tau_{t},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta_{x}=-\beta\xi_{x}+\frac{\beta}{2}\tau_{t}+(\beta^{2}-\gamma)\xi_{u},\hskip 10.00002pt(\beta^{2}-\gamma)(2\xi_{x}-\beta\xi_{u}-\tau_{t})=0. (24)

The cross differentiation of the two first equations in (24) implies (β2−γ)​ξu​u=0(\beta^{2}-\gamma)\xi_{uu}=0. Then the separate differentiations of the last equation in (24) with respect to xx and uu successively give (β2−γ)​ξx​u=0(\beta^{2}-\gamma)\xi_{xu}=0 and (β2−γ)​ξx​x=0(\beta^{2}-\gamma)\xi_{xx}=0. In view of these equations for ξ\xi, the same differentiation of the two first equations in (24) results in ηx​x=−β​ξx​x\eta_{xx}=-\beta\xi_{xx}, ηx​u=−β​ξx​u\eta_{xu}=-\beta\xi_{xu} and ηu​u=−β​ξu​u\eta_{uu}=-\beta\xi_{uu}. Therefore, if γ≠β2\gamma\neq\beta^{2}, then we have the required determining equations.

Suppose that γ=β2\gamma=\beta^{2}. Then β≠0\beta\neq 0, and modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence we can set β=1\beta=1, i.e., f=(ux+1)−2f=(u_{x}+1)^{-2}. The general solution of the system ηx=−ξx+τt/2\eta_{x}=-\xi_{x}+\tau_{t}/2, ηu=−ξu+τt/2\eta_{u}=-\xi_{u}+\tau_{t}/2 with respect to η\eta is η=−ξ+τt​(u+x)/2+η0​(t)\eta=-\xi+\tau_{t}(u+x)/2+\eta^{0}(t), where η0\eta^{0} is an arbitrary smooth function of tt. For these values of ff and η\eta, the determining equation (20b) takes the form

((ξt+ξug)ux+ηgu+(τt−ηu)g−ηt)(ux+1)=ξu​uux+22ξx​uux+ξx​x\big((\xi_{t}+\xi_{u}g)u_{x}+\eta g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta_{u})g-\eta_{t}\big)(u_{x}+1)=\xi_{uu}u_{x}{}^{\!2}+2\xi_{xu}u_{x}+\xi_{xx}

and splits with respect to uxu_{x} into the system

ξt+ξu​g=ξu​u,η​gu+(τt−ηu)​g−ηt=ξx​x,ξu​u−2​ξx​u+ξx​x=0.\displaystyle\xi_{t}+\xi_{u}g=\xi_{uu},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta_{u})g-\eta_{t}=\xi_{xx},\hskip 10.00002pt\xi_{uu}-2\xi_{xu}+\xi_{xx}=0. (25)

The last equation can be represented as (∂x−∂u)2ξ=0(\partial_{x}-\partial_{u})^{2}\xi=0, and hence its general solution is ξ=ξ1​(t,ω)​u+ξ0​(t,ω)\xi=\xi^{1}(t,\omega)u+\xi^{0}(t,\omega), where ξ1\xi^{1} and ξ0\xi^{0} are arbitrary smooth functions of tt and ω=x+u\omega=x+u. In view of the derived expressions for ξ\xi and η\eta, the system of the first two equations of (25) reduces to the system

ξt1​u+ξt0+(ξω1​u+ξ1+ξω0)​g=ξω​ω1​u+2​ξω1+ξω​ω0,\displaystyle\xi^{1}_{t}u+\xi^{0}_{t}+(\xi^{1}_{\omega}u+\xi^{1}+\xi^{0}_{\omega})g=\xi^{1}_{\omega\omega}u+2\xi^{1}_{\omega}+\xi^{0}_{\omega\omega}, (26)
(−2​ξ1​u−2​ξ0+τt​ω+2​η0)​gu+τt​g+4​ξω1−τt​t​ω−2​ηt0=0.\displaystyle(-2\xi^{1}u-2\xi^{0}+\tau_{t}\omega+2\eta^{0})g_{u}+\tau_{t}g+4\xi^{1}_{\omega}-\tau_{tt}\omega-2\eta^{0}_{t}=0. (27)

We assume (t,ω,u)(t,\omega,u) to be the tuple of independent variables in the last system.

If the arbitrary element gg is not a fractional linear function, then we can split the equation (26) simultaneously with respect to gg an uu and obtain the equations ξω1=0\xi^{1}_{\omega}=0 and ξω0=−ξ1\xi^{0}_{\omega}=-\xi^{1}, whose consequence is ξω​ω0=0\xi^{0}_{\omega\omega}=0. Otherwise (i.e., in the case of nonconstant fractional linear gg, since gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0 by a lemma’s assumption), we differentiate the equation (27) with respect to ω\omega and split the derived differential consequence with respect to uu, which again leads to the equations ξω1=0\xi^{1}_{\omega}=0 and ξω​ω0=0\xi^{0}_{\omega\omega}=0. Therefore, in the third case we also have the required equations ξx​x=ξx​u=ξu​u=0\xi_{xx}=\xi_{xu}=\xi_{uu}=0 and, therefore, ηx​x=ηx​u=ηu​u=0\eta_{xx}=\eta_{xu}=\eta_{uu}=0. ∎

In other words, the system of determining equations for Lie symmetries of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} in fact reduces to the system of the equations τx=τu=0\tau_{x}=\tau_{u}=0, (20a), (21) and

ξt+ξu​g=0,\displaystyle\xi_{t}+\xi_{u}g=0, (28)
η​gu+(τt−ηu)​g−ηt=0.\displaystyle\eta g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta_{u})g-\eta_{t}=0. (29)

The system (21) is equivalent to the following representation for the components ξ\xi and η\eta:

ξ=ξ1​(t)​x+ξ2​(t)​u+ξ0​(t),η=η1​(t)​x+η2​(t)​u+η0​(t),\displaystyle\xi=\xi^{1}(t)x+\xi^{2}(t)u+\xi^{0}(t),\hskip 10.00002pt\eta=\eta^{1}(t)x+\eta^{2}(t)u+\eta^{0}(t),

where ξ0\xi^{0}, ξ1\xi^{1}, ξ2\xi^{2}, η0\eta^{0}, η1\eta^{1}, and η2\eta^{2} are smooth functions of tt.

Lemma 16.

(i) For all equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, except those Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalent to equations of Case 1, the xx-components of admitted Lie-symmetry vector fields satisfy the determining equation ξu=0\xi_{u}=0. (ii) For all equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}, except those Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalent to equations of Case 1, the uu-components of admitted Lie-symmetry vector fields satisfy the determining equation ηx=0\eta_{x}=0.

Proof.

Suppose that an equation 𝔈\mathfrak{E} in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} admits a Lie-symmetry vector field QQ with (ξ2,η1)≠(0,0)(\xi^{2},\eta^{1})\neq(0,0), and (f,g)(f,g) is the associated value of the arbitrary-element tuple.

If ξu=ξ2≠0\xi_{u}=\xi^{2}\neq 0 (resp. ηx=η1≠0\eta_{x}=\eta^{1}\neq 0) for QQ, then the equation (28) (resp. the differential consequence of (29) obtained with the action by the operator ∂x\partial_{x}) implies gu​u=0g_{uu}=0, and hence g=umodGℛ∼g=u\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} since gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0 in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For this value of the arbitrary element gg, the equations (28) and (29) respectively split with respect to (x,u)(x,u) into the equations

ξ0t=ξ1t=0,ξ2t=−ξ2andη0t=η0,η1t=η1,η2t=τt.\displaystyle\xi^{0}_{t}=\xi^{1}_{t}=0,\hskip 10.00002pt\xi^{2}_{t}=-\xi^{2}\hskip 10.00002pt\mbox{and}\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{0}_{t}=\eta^{0},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{1}_{t}=\eta^{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{2}_{t}=\tau_{t}. (30)

Now we apply the furcate splitting with respect to ff. Here the template form of equations for ff is

(a1ux+2a2ux+a3)fux+(2a1ux+a4)f=0,\displaystyle(a_{1}u_{x}{}^{\!2}+a_{2}u_{x}+a_{3})f_{u_{x}}+(2a_{1}u_{x}+a_{4})f=0, (31)

where a1a_{1}, …, a4a_{4} are constants. Template-form equations for ff are obtained by fixing tt in the classifying equation (20a). Denote by kk the number of linearly independent tuples (a1,a2,a3,a4)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}) among those associated with template-form equations for ff. We have k>0k>0 since (ξ2,η1)≠(0,0)(\xi^{2},\eta^{1})\neq(0,0) for the Lie-symmetry vector field QQ.

If k⩾2k\geqslant 2, then f=ε​(ux+1)−2modGℛ∼f=\varepsilon(u_{x}+1)^{-2}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} with ε=±1\varepsilon=\pm 1 since fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0 and (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 for equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Splitting the equation (20a) for this value of ff with respect to uxu_{x}, we derive the equations τt=2​η1+2​ξ1\tau_{t}=2\eta^{1}+2\xi^{1} and R:=ξ1−ξ2+η1−η2=0R:=\xi^{1}-\xi^{2}+\eta^{1}-\eta^{2}=0. Then in view of the system (30), we have τt​t=2​η1\tau_{tt}=2\eta^{1}, Rt​t=−ξ2+η1=0R_{tt}=-\xi^{2}+\eta^{1}=0 and Rt​t​t=ξ2+η1=0R_{ttt}=\xi^{2}+\eta^{1}=0, i.e., ξ2=η1=0\xi^{2}=\eta^{1}=0 for Lie-symmetry vector fields of the equation 𝔈\mathfrak{E}, which contradicts the condition (ξ2,η1)≠(0,0)(\xi^{2},\eta^{1})\neq(0,0) for QQ.

Therefore, k=1k=1. We fix a template-form equation, and let (a1,a2,a3,a4)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}) be the corresponding (nonzero) coefficient tuple. Since k=1k=1, the coefficient tuple (−ξ2,η2−ξ1,η1,τt−2​ξ1)(-\xi^{2},\eta^{2}-\xi^{1},\eta^{1},\tau_{t}-2\xi^{1}) of the equation (20a) is proportional to (a1,a2,a3,a4)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}),

−ξ2=λ​a1,η2−ξ1=λ​a2,η1=λ​a3,τt−2​ξ1=λ​a4,\displaystyle-\xi^{2}=\lambda a_{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{2}-\xi^{1}=\lambda a_{2},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{1}=\lambda a_{3},\hskip 10.00002pt\tau_{t}-2\xi^{1}=\lambda a_{4}, (32)

where λ=λ⁡(t)\lambda=\lambda(t) is a nonvanishing smooth function of tt, and (a1,a3)≠(0,0)(a_{1},a_{3})\neq(0,0) since (ξ2,η1)≠(0,0)(\xi^{2},\eta^{1})\neq(0,0) for QQ. This implies that a1​η1+a3​ξ2=0a_{1}\eta^{1}+a_{3}\xi^{2}=0. The differentiation of this equation with respect to tt gives, in view of (30), the equation a1​η1−a3​ξ2=0a_{1}\eta^{1}-a_{3}\xi^{2}=0, i.e., a1​η1=a3​ξ2=0a_{1}\eta^{1}=a_{3}\xi^{2}=0 and thus ξ2​η1=a1​a3=0\xi^{2}\eta^{1}=a_{1}a_{3}=0.

If a1≠0a_{1}\neq 0, then due to the possibility of simultaneous opposite scalings of (a1,a2,a3,a4)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}) and λ\lambda we can assume without loss of generality that a1=1a_{1}=1 and λ=−ξ2≠0\lambda=-\xi^{2}\neq 0. Hence η1=0\eta^{1}=0 and a3=0a_{3}=0. The other equations following from (32) are η2=−a2​ξ2+ξ1\eta^{2}=-a_{2}\xi^{2}+\xi^{1} and τt=−a4​ξ2+2​ξ1\tau_{t}=-a_{4}\xi^{2}+2\xi^{1}. We combine them with equations of (30) to get τt=ηt2=a2​ξ2\tau_{t}=\eta^{2}_{t}=a_{2}\xi^{2}, which leads to a4=−a2a_{4}=-a_{2} and ξ1=0\xi^{1}=0. We have a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0 since otherwise the fixed template-form equation for ff contradicts the auxiliary inequality (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 for arbitrary elements of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This is why modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence we can set a2=1a_{2}=1 and obtain, after alternating the sign of tt if ε=−1\varepsilon=-1, Case 1.

For the case a3≠0a_{3}\neq 0, the consideration is similar. Due to the possibility of simultaneous opposite scalings of (a1,a2,a3,a4)(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4}) and λ\lambda we can assume without loss of generality that a3=1a_{3}=1 and λ=η1≠0\lambda=\eta^{1}\neq 0. Hence ξ2=0\xi^{2}=0 and a1=0a_{1}=0. The other equations following from (32) are η2=a2​η1+ξ1\eta^{2}=a_{2}\eta^{1}+\xi^{1} and τt=a4​η1+2​ξ1\tau_{t}=a_{4}\eta^{1}+2\xi^{1}. We combine them with equations of (30) to obtain τt=ηt2=a2​η1\tau_{t}=\eta^{2}_{t}=a_{2}\eta^{1}, which leads to a4=a2a_{4}=a_{2} and ξ1=0\xi^{1}=0. We have a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0 since otherwise the fixed template-form equation for ff contradicts the auxiliary inequality fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0 for arbitrary elements of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. This is why modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence we can set a2=1a_{2}=1 and obtain, after alternating the sign of tt if ε=−1\varepsilon=-1, Case 1. ∎

Therefore, in the rest of the proof we can exclude equations falling, modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence, into Cases 1 or 1 and additionally set ξt=ξu=ηx=0\xi_{t}=\xi_{u}=\eta_{x}=0, i.e.,

ξ=c1​x+c2,η=η2​(t)​u+η0​(t),\xi=c_{1}x+c_{2},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta=\eta^{2}(t)u+\eta^{0}(t),

where c1c_{1} and c2c_{2} are constants. The unsolved determining equations are exhausted by the reduced form of the equations (20a) and (29),

(η2−c1)​ux​fux+(τt−2​c1)​f=0,\displaystyle(\eta^{2}-c_{1})u_{x}f_{u_{x}}+(\tau_{t}-2c_{1})f=0, (33)
(η2​u+η0)​gu+(τt−η2)​g=ηt2​u+ηt0.\displaystyle(\eta^{2}u+\eta^{0})g_{u}+(\tau_{t}-\eta^{2})g=\eta^{2}_{t}u+\eta^{0}_{t}. (34)

We complete the group classification of the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} by the method of furcate splitting. The system of the reduced classifying equations (33) and (34) is decoupled, and the arbitrary elements ff and gg are unary functions of different arguments. Thus, we need to apply two-step furcate splitting, with respect to ff and then with respect to gg. Here the template forms of equations for ff and gg are respectively

a2​ux​fux+a4​f=0,\displaystyle a_{2}u_{x}f_{u_{x}}+a_{4}f=0, (35)
(b1​u+b2)​gu+b3​g=b4​u+b5,\displaystyle(b_{1}u+b_{2})g_{u}+b_{3}g=b_{4}u+b_{5}, (36)

where a2a_{2}, a4a_{4} and b1b_{1}, …, b5b_{5} are constants. (We number the constants a2a_{2} and a4a_{4} in the way consistent with the template form (31).) Template-form equations for ff and gg are obtained by fixing tt in the classifying equations (33) and (34), respectively. Denote by kk (resp. ll) the number of linearly independent tuples (a2,a4)(a_{2},a_{4}) (resp. (b1,…,b5)(b_{1},\dots,b_{5})) among those associated with template-form equations for ff (resp. gg). We have k<2k<2 since f≠0f\neq 0.

𝒌=𝟎\boldsymbol{k=0}. This means that the equation (33) is an identity with respect to ff, i.e., η2=c1\eta^{2}=c_{1} and τt=2​c1\tau_{t}=2c_{1}. Then b3=b1b_{3}=b_{1} and b4=0b_{4}=0 in the template form (36) of equations for gg. The number ll of linearly independent tuples among possible values of the coefficient tuple (b1,b2,b5)(b_{1},b_{2},b_{5}) cannot exceed one since otherwise the corresponding system of template-form equations either is inconsistent or has only constant solutions, which contradicts the auxiliary inequality gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0 for arbitrary elements of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. If l=0l=0, i.e., the classifying equation (34) is also an identity, then we get the general classification Case 1 of Table 1 with no Lie symmetry extension. For l=1l=1, depending on whether or not the coefficient b1b_{1} in a nonidentical template-form equation vanishes, we obtain that either g=umodGℛ∼g=u\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} or g=u−1+νmodGℛ∼g=u^{-1}+\nu\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}. The first option corresponds to Case 1. The second option leads to Case 1 in view of the condition ν=0\nu=0 since for ν≠0\nu\neq 0 we only obtain the kernel invariance algebra 𝔤𝒞∩=⟨∂t,∂x⟩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{C}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x}\rangle, which corresponds to the condition l=0l=0 contradicting the supposed condition l=1l=1.

𝒌=𝟏.\boldsymbol{k=1.} We fix a (nonidentical) template-form equation for ff, and let (a2,a4)(a_{2},a_{4}) be the corresponding (nonzero) coefficient tuple. The inequality f≠0f\neq 0 implies a2≠0a_{2}\neq 0, and thus we can set a2=1a_{2}=1. Denote n:=−a4n:=-a_{4}. Then the equation (35) implies that f=|ux|nmodGℛ∼f=|u_{x}|^{n}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}, where n≠0n\neq 0 and n≠−2n\neq-2 according to the auxiliary inequalities fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0 and (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 for arbitrary elements of equations in the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. Since k=1k=1, the coefficient tuple (η2−c1,τt−2​c1)(\eta^{2}-c_{1},\tau_{t}-2c_{1}) of the equation (33) is proportional to (1,−n)(1,-n). In other words, η2−c1=λ\eta^{2}-c_{1}=\lambda, τt−2​c1=−n​λ\tau_{t}-2c_{1}=-n\lambda, where λ=λ⁡(t)\lambda=\lambda(t) is a nonvanishing smooth function of tt. Hence τt=−n​η2+(n+2)​c1\tau_{t}=-n\eta^{2}+(n+2)c_{1}, and the equation (34) takes the form

(η2​u+η0)​gu+((n+2)​c1−(n+1)​η2)​g=ηt2​u+ηt0.\displaystyle(\eta^{2}u+\eta^{0})g_{u}+\big((n+2)c_{1}-(n+1)\eta^{2}\big)g=\eta^{2}_{t}u+\eta^{0}_{t}. (37)

We again apply the furcate splitting with respect to gg using the number ll for marking different cases. We have l>0l>0 since otherwise the equation (37) would be an identity with respect to gg and thus η0=η2=0\eta^{0}=\eta^{2}=0 and, in view of n≠−2n\neq-2, c1=0c_{1}=0, which would lead to the kernel invariance algebra 𝔤𝒞∩=⟨∂t,∂x⟩\mathfrak{g}^{\cap}_{\mathcal{C}}=\langle\partial_{t},\,\partial_{x}\rangle and would thus give k=0k=0, contradicting the condition k=1k=1. The further consideration splits into two cases, l⩾2l\geqslant 2 and l=1l=1.

l⩾2l\geqslant 2. Note that three is the maximal value of ll since for greater values of ll, systems of template-form equations are not consistent.

Suppose that for two template-form equations with linearly independent tuples of coefficients (b1,…,b5)(b_{1},\dots,b_{5}) and (b1′,…,b5′)(b_{1}^{\prime},\dots,b_{5}^{\prime}), the conditions b2​b1′−b2′​b1≠0b_{2}b_{1}^{\prime}-b_{2}^{\prime}b_{1}\neq 0, b3​b1′−b3′​b1=0b_{3}b_{1}^{\prime}-b_{3}^{\prime}b_{1}=0 and b4​b1′−b4′​b1≠0b_{4}b_{1}^{\prime}-b_{4}^{\prime}b_{1}\neq 0 hold. Then the consistency of these template-form equations implies that gu​u​u=0g_{uuu}=0 and gu​u≠0g_{uu}\neq 0, i.e., g=u2+δmodGℛ∼g=u^{2}+\delta\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} with δ∈{−1,0,1}\delta\in\{-1,0,1\}. Splitting the equation (37) for the obtained value of the arbitrary element gg with respect to uu, we derive the equations (n+2)​c1=(n−1)​η2(n+2)c_{1}=(n-1)\eta^{2}, ηt0=−2​δ​η2\eta^{0}_{t}=-2\delta\eta^{2} and ηt2=2​η0\eta^{2}_{t}=2\eta^{0}. These equations imply n=1n=1 since otherwise η2=(n+2)​c1/(n−1)\eta^{2}=(n+2)c_{1}/(n-1), η0=0\eta^{0}=0, δ​c1=0\delta c_{1}=0 and thus l⩽1l\leqslant 1, which contradicts the assumed condition l⩾2l\geqslant 2. Then c1=0c_{1}=0, and we obtain Cases 1a, 1b and 1c depending on the value of δ\delta.

If there exists a pair of template-form equations with other conditions on the associated linearly independent tuples of coefficients bb’s and b′b^{\prime}’s, then we get gu​u=0g_{uu}=0, i.e., g=ε​umodGℛ∼g=\varepsilon u\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} with ε∈{−1,1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\} in view of the auxiliary inequality gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0 within the class 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The equation (37) with this value of gg splits into the equations ηt2=−ε​n​η2+ε⁡(n+2)​c1\eta^{2}_{t}=-\varepsilon n\eta^{2}+\varepsilon(n+2)c_{1} and ηt0=ε​η0\eta^{0}_{t}=\varepsilon\eta^{0}. As a result, we get Case 1b, for which in fact l=3l=3.

l=1.l=1. Then the coefficient tuple of the equation (37) is proportional to the (nonvanishing) coefficient tuple of a template-form equation,

η2=χ​b1,η0=χ​b2,(n+2)​c1−(n+1)​η2=χ​b3,−ηt2=χ​b4,−ηt0=χ​b5.\eta^{2}=\chi b_{1},\hskip 10.00002pt\eta^{0}=\chi b_{2},\hskip 10.00002pt(n+2)c_{1}-(n+1)\eta^{2}=\chi b_{3},\hskip 10.00002pt-\eta^{2}_{t}=\chi b_{4},\hskip 10.00002pt-\eta^{0}_{t}=\chi b_{5}.

χ=χ⁡(t)\chi=\chi(t) is a nonvanishing smooth function of tt. Moreover, we have the inequality gu​u≠0g_{uu}\neq 0 since otherwise l=2l=2. We consider separately two cases, (b1,b4)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{4})\neq(0,0) and b1=b4=0b_{1}=b_{4}=0.

Suppose at first that (b1,b4)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{4})\neq(0,0). We recombine the above equations to the equations b1​χt+b4​χ=0b_{1}\chi_{t}+b_{4}\chi=0 and b2​χt+b5​χ=0b_{2}\chi_{t}+b_{5}\chi=0 whose consistency as algebraic equations with respect to (χt,χ)(\chi_{t},\chi) implies that the pair (b2,b5)(b_{2},b_{5}) is proportional to (b1,b4)(b_{1},b_{4}). Therefore, modulo Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence (more specifically, modulo shifts of uu) we can set b2=b5=0b_{2}=b_{5}=0, and thus η0=0\eta^{0}=0. Then it becomes obvious that b1≠0b_{1}\neq 0 since otherwise b3​b4≠0b_{3}b_{4}\neq 0, which implies gu​u=0g_{uu}=0. Therefore, due to the possibility of simultaneous opposite scalings of (b1,b3,b4)(b_{1},b_{3},b_{4}) and χ\chi we can assume without loss of generality that b1=1b_{1}=1 and χ=η2≠0\chi=\eta^{2}\neq 0. Hence (n+2)​c1=(n+1+b3)​η2(n+2)c_{1}=(n+1+b_{3})\eta^{2} and ηt2=−b4​η2\eta^{2}_{t}=-b_{4}\eta^{2}. For b4=0b_{4}=0 we directly obtain Case 1a. If b4≠0b_{4}\neq 0, then c1=0c_{1}=0 and b3=−n−1b_{3}=-n-1, which gives Case 1b.

Let b1=b4=0b_{1}=b_{4}=0. Then the inequality gu​u≠0g_{uu}\neq 0 implies b2≠0b_{2}\neq 0 and b5=0b_{5}=0. To derive the last equality, we use the fact that otherwise ηt0=b2​χt≠0\eta^{0}_{t}=b_{2}\chi_{t}\neq 0 and hence b3=0b_{3}=0, which contradicts the inequality gu​u≠0g_{uu}\neq 0. Therefore, g=ε​eumodGℛ∼g=\varepsilon e^{u}\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}} with ε∈{−1,1}\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}, which gives Case 1.

The proof of Proposition 14 is completed.

6 Lie reductions and exact solutions

Exact solutions of equations for the class ℋ\mathcal{H} were constructed by various methods in many papers, including classical Lie reductions [10], nonclassical reductions using conditional symmetries [4, 9, 12, 44, 47] and generalized separation of variables [13]. See also [3, Section 10.5], [34, Chapter 5] and references therein.

The construction of exact solutions of equations from the class ℱ\mathcal{F} is reduced by the family of transformations from Gℱ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} with (t,x,u)(t,x,u)-components t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=x\tilde{x}=x, u~=u−g​t\tilde{u}=u-gt, which is parameterized by the arbitrary element gg, to the same problem for the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, cf. Section 2. Equations from the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, which are nonlinear filtration equations, are potential equations of nonlinear diffusion equations. Lie reductions of the latter equations were studied in [30]. Exact solutions of both nonlinear diffusion equations and nonlinear filtration equations were found using Lie and quasilocal (potential) symmetries [1, 2], generalized separation of variables [7, 11], nonclassical reductions and nonclassical potential reductions [5, 15, 42] and generalized conditional symmetries [43]. See also [3, Section 10.2], [34, Chapter 5] and references therein.

The optimal way for constructing exact solutions of equations from the class ℒ\mathcal{L} is to use their linearization by the hodograph transformation t~=t\tilde{t}=t, x~=u\tilde{x}=u, u~=x\tilde{u}=x with (t~,x~)(\tilde{t},\tilde{x}) and u~\tilde{u} being the new independent and dependent variables, respectively, to Kolmogorov equations; see the introduction.

This is why it is justified to look for exact solutions of equations from the class 𝒞\mathcal{C} only, excluding equations related to Case 1b, which is similar to Case 1a with respect to additional equivalence transformations. We select all 𝒢ℛ∼\mathcal{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-inequivalent cases of Table 1 with four-dimensional maximal Lie invariance algebras as the most interesting, which are Cases 1, 1a and 1. They are the obvious contenders for allowing one to construct nontrivial explicit solutions. We identify the structure of the associated maximal Lie algebras according Mubarakzyanov’s classification of real four-dimensional Lie algebras [22]. Optimal lists of subalgebras of such algebras (i.e., complete lists of subalgebras that are inequivalent up to inner automorphisms of the corresponding algebras) were constructed by Patera and Winternitz in [32]. Since we carry out Lie reductions of partial differential equations with two independent variables to ordinary differential equations, we only need optimal lists of one-dimensional subalgebras. For each of the selected classification cases, we additionally gauge, whenever it is possible, subalgebra parameters using outer automorphisms of the corresponding algebras that are induced by discrete symmetries of related equations. See also [36] for a collection of various characteristics of low-dimensional Lie algebras and of classifications of related objects. It is convenient to present the results of Lie reductions as Table 2, each row of which includes a basis element of the canonical representative of an equivalence class of one-dimensional subalgebras, an associated ansatz for the dependent variable, the invariant independent variable ω\omega and the corresponding reduced equation, respectively. Here and below cc’s are arbitrary constants.

ut=ux​xux+1+ε​u,ε=±1modGℛ∼,\displaystyle u_{t}=\frac{u_{xx}}{u_{x}+1}+\varepsilon u,\hskip 10.00002pt\varepsilon=\pm 1\bmod G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}, (38)

Case 1. Up to Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence, this is the only case among cases of Lie-symmetry extensions within the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} that admits non-fiber-preserving point symmetry transformations. (Such symmetry transformations are typical for equations from the subclasses ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℒ\mathcal{L}.) The indication, in infinitesimal terms, of the presence of such symmetry transformations is that the xx-component of the Lie-symmetry vector field e−ε​t(∂t−εu∂x+εu∂u)e^{-\varepsilon t}(\partial_{t}-\varepsilon u\partial_{x}+\varepsilon u\partial_{u}) of this case depends on uu. Note that the further hodograph transformation t^=t~\hat{t}=\tilde{t}, x^=u~\hat{x}=\tilde{u}, u^=x~\hat{u}=\tilde{x} reduces the equation (41) to the equation u^t^=u^x^−3​u^x^​x^+ε​x\hat{u}_{\hat{t}}=\hat{u}_{\hat{x}}^{-3}\hat{u}_{\hat{x}\hat{x}}+\varepsilon x, which is the potential equation for the nonlinear diffusion–reaction equations u˘t^=(u˘−3​u˘x^)x^+ε\breve{u}_{\hat{t}}=(\breve{u}^{-3}\breve{u}_{\hat{x}})_{\hat{x}}+\varepsilon, where u˘=u^x^\breve{u}=\hat{u}_{\hat{x}}. See the first paragraph of this section for references on symmetry analysis of the last equation.

7 Conclusion

Carrying out group classification of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} of (1+1)-dimensional nonlinear diffusion–reaction equations with gradient-dependent diffusivity in the present paper, we have corrected and enhanced results of [8] in several aspects.

We have justified the necessity of studying the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R} and carefully analyzed its structure. In the notation of the present paper, the authors of [8] considered the group classification problem only for the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} with respect to its equivalence group, having discarded other subclasses of ℛ\mathcal{R}. They include the subclass ℋ\mathcal{H} with known group classification, the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} whose group classification can be easily derived from known group classification of the subclass ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and the subclass ℒ\mathcal{L} of linearizable equations with transformational properties essentially different from other equations in the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. Nevertheless, the consideration of the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} alone is not natural since some equations in 𝒞\mathcal{C} are related by point transformations to equations in ℱ\mathcal{F}, and the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F} intersects the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H} and ℒ\mathcal{L}.

We have computed the usual equivalence groups of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and all the above subclasses as well as the generalized equivalence group G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} and the effective generalized equivalence group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}. We have also checked the consistency of these groups for using in the course of group classification. The group G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} gives the first nontrivial example of finite-dimensional effective generalized equivalence group in the literature. Moreover, the class ℱ\mathcal{F} has another unexpected property formulated in Theorem 7: any effective generalized equivalence group of the class ℱ\mathcal{F} does not contain the usual equivalence group of this class. This phenomenon had not been observed before, and finding out it is the most interesting result of the present paper although it was obtained as a by-product. Since G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is not a normal subgroup of G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}}, it is obvious that G^ℱ∼\hat{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is not a unique effective generalized equivalence group of the subclass ℱ\mathcal{F}. Whether this group is unique up to the subgroup similarity within G¯ℱ∼\bar{G}^{\sim}_{\mathcal{F}} is still an open problem.

In the context of the group classification of the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} given in [8], the most significant and also unexpected enhancement is discovering Case 1, which was missed in [8]. It essentially differs from the other classification cases in the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C} since only equations fitting in Case 1 up to Gℛ∼G^{\sim}_{\mathcal{R}}-equivalence admits non-fiber-preserving Lie-symmetry transformations. An explanation of the presence of such transformations is that these equations are reduced by non-fiber-preserving point transformations to a potential nonlinear diffusion–reaction equation.

The third direction of enhancements concerns additional equivalences between classification cases. We have constructed additional equivalence transformations relating Cases 1a–1c, which were missed in [8]. It is obvious that there also exist similar transformations between multidimensional counterparts of Cases 1a–1c, cf. Cases 6–8 of [8, Table 2]. Using relevant equivalence relations, we have properly gauged all constants parameterizing classification cases and first proved the completeness of the additional equivalence transformations presented in the footnote of Table 1, which leads to the group classification of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} up to the general point equivalence, see Theorem 13.

The complex structure of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} required the application of various advanced techniques of group analysis of differential equations. Moreover, we needed to combine and develop them for an efficient solution of the group classification problem for the class ℛ\mathcal{R}. At the same time, the simple form of equations in this class has allowed us to present the obtained results in a clear way.

Results of Section 2 on various equivalence groups of the class ℛ\mathcal{R} and of its subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L}, ℱ\mathcal{F}, ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} and the classification of Lie symmetries of equations from these classes that is presented in Section 3 jointly imply that these classes are not normalized in both the usual and the generalized sense. (See [28, 35, 39] for related definitions.) The existence of additional equivalence transformations among cases of Lie-symmetries extension in the subclasses ℋ\mathcal{H}, ℒ\mathcal{L} and 𝒞\mathcal{C} means that these subclasses as well as the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R} are even not semi-normalized. This is why in the course of computing the above equivalence groups, we have suggested and applied an optimized version of the direct method. This version involves preliminary study of admissible transformations within the entire class and the successive splitting of the determining equations for these transformations with respect to the corresponding arbitrary elements and their derivatives, depending on auxiliary constraints associated with each of the subclasses under consideration separately. In order to make the group classifications of the subclasses ℱ\mathcal{F} and ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} consistent, we have found the generalized equivalence group of ℱ\mathcal{F} and its effective counterpart. The group classification of the class ℒ\mathcal{L} has been obtained from the known group classification of Kolmogorov equations up to general point equivalence [40, Corollary 7] using a technique based on mappings between classes of differential equations via point transformations [47].

The arbitrary elements ff and gg depend on different arguments, uxu_{x} and uu, respectively. This is why in the course of solving the group classification problem for the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}, we needed to use the double furcate splitting with respect to two pairs “(an argument, an arbitrary element)”, (ux,f)(u_{x},f) and (u,g)(u,g). Moreover, it is impossible to directly apply furcate splitting to the classifying system (20) within the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}, not to mention the entire class ℛ\mathcal{R}. The subsystem of non-classifying determining equations for Lie symmetries of equations from the class ℛ\mathcal{R} is exhausted by two equations, which are common for all (1+1)-dimensional evolution equations and constrain only the tt-components of Lie-symmetry vector fields, τx=τu=0\tau_{x}=\tau_{u}=0. The dependence of the corresponding xx- and uu-components on uu is not specified and hence the furcate splitting with respect to (u,g)(u,g) cannot be initiated without additional constraints on the arbitrary elements and without a preliminary preparation of the classifying equations. One more complication is that the classifying system (20) is (partially) coupled in (f,g)(f,g). Under the auxiliary inequalities fux≠0f_{u_{x}}\neq 0, (ux​f2)ux≠0(u_{x}{}^{\!2}f)_{u_{x}}\neq 0 and gu≠0g_{u}\neq 0 singling out the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}, the system (20) implies more equations, (21), not involving the arbitrary elements (f,g)(f,g) and thus reduces to an uncoupled system for (f,g)(f,g); see Lemma 15 and the discussion after it. An inconvenience of the reduced system is that it includes two equations for gg, (28) and (29). Then we have found out a property of Lie symmetry algebras that singles out two classification cases being singular in the subclass 𝒞\mathcal{C}, Cases 1 and 1. In the course of computing these cases, we use the auxiliary furcate spitting with respect (ux,f)(u_{x},f). For other classification cases, there are very restrictive determining equations, ξt=ξu=ηx=0\xi_{t}=\xi_{u}=\eta_{x}=0, which simplify the system of classifying equations to the uncoupled systems of only two equations (33) and (34). The last system is perfectly appropriate for the double furcate splitting with respect to (ux,f)(u_{x},f) and (u,g)(u,g).

For effectively constructing additional equivalence transformations or for proving nonexistence of such transformations, we have combined the direct method of computing point transformations between similar equations with the algebraic method based on comparing the structure of the corresponding Lie invariance algebras.
